catalogTitle: Marriage: Giving the Ring - A Symbol of the Essence of Marriage

oneLiner.en: Speaking to a chassan and kallah during their sheva brachos, the Mashgiach explains that marriage, like Shabbos the bride of Knesses Yisrael, is built on giving, and that the ring of kiddushin is the first act of that giving.

abstract.en: The Mashgiach opens with Adam and Chava, created as one and then separated, and explains that every chassan finds the kallah he was once one with. Shabbos too is a bride: Hashem gave her Knesses Yisrael as her partner, and since Shabbos is pure neshamah, souls can unite with her. The seven days of sheva brachos are the couple's own Shabbos, and the seventh bracha unites the chassan and kallah with Yerushalayim, the bereaved kallah. Turning to kiddushin, he asks why Beis Hillel allows a mere perutah, and answers that kiddushin is the start of a life of giving: what counts is not what one gives but how, with respect. Nesuin itself means giving. The kallah, silent and passive, gives the greatest gift, herself, just as Shabbos seems to take yet gives all brachos. He brings the Rambam's directions for husband and wife, describes how mutual giving builds happiness, and closes by urging the couple to learn their two heritages together, reading from Rav Hirsch on Shabbos.

en: Every chassan and kallah were one in Adam and Chava, and Hashem reunites them in one house.
Shabbos is the kallah of Knesses Yisrael, and the seven days of sheva brachos are the couple's own Shabbos.
Kiddushin is the first act of giving, and what counts is not how much one gives but how, with respect.
Nesuin means giving: the husband commits himself to give all his life without thinking of taking.
The kallah's silent passivity at kiddushin is the highest giving: she gives her very self.
Following the Rambam's directions, each spouse's giving draws out the other's, and that is the secret of a happy home.

title.en: Adam, Chava and Shabbos the bride

summary.en: The Mashgiach describes Adam and Chava, created as one person and then separated, as the roots of every chassan and kallah. He then brings the Midrash that Shabbos complained it had no partner and was given Knesses Yisrael, so that the Jewish people are joined to Shabbos and separated from it each week.

title.en: The seven days as the couple's Shabbos

summary.en: The Mashgiach asks how human beings can be wed to Shabbos, a unit of time, and answers that Shabbos is pure neshamah, the soul of Knesses Yisrael. He explains that the seven days of sheva brachos are a private Shabbos given to the chassan and kallah, with song, rest and seven brachos, and that the seventh day is a double Shabbos.

title.en: Yerushalayim, the waiting kallah

summary.en: The Mashgiach describes Yerushalayim as a kallah with a heavy heart, waiting for the redemption, and explains that the sheva brachos give her her own bracha before the bracha for the new chassan and kallah. The seventh bracha, the Shabbos of the brachos, unites them all, as they will all be united in the day that is entirely Shabbos.

title.en: Dinar or perutah: what kiddushin is

summary.en: Turning to the moment of kiddushin, the Mashgiach brings the dispute of Beis Shammai, who require a dinar for the dignity of a Jewish daughter, and Beis Hillel, who allow a perutah, and asks why Beis Hillel would disagree. He rejects seeing kiddushin as a purchase and brings an essay that a person is perfect when he gives, and that a marriage succeeds only while both are conscious that they married in order to give.

title.en: Not what he gives but how

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that kiddushin opens married life with an act of giving. Beis Shammai want the giving to cost, while Beis Hillel teach that it is not what one gives but how: a perutah given with the awareness that the kallah is Shabbos and Yerushalayim is worth more than all treasures. The kesubah's promise of respect and the word nesuin, which he reads as giving, carry the same idea.

title.en: The kallah gives herself

summary.en: The Mashgiach asks why the kallah gives nothing and says nothing at kiddushin, and explains that by making herself passive she gives her very self, the highest giving. To the question whether this is slavery he answers from Shabbos, which seems only to take yet is the source of all brachos, and explains that a woman, bound to the Shechinah, can give in a way a man cannot; Jewishness itself comes from the mother.

title.en: The Rambam's plan for a happy home

summary.en: Answering those who oppose this view, the Mashgiach reads the Rambam in Hilchos Ishus: the husband honors his wife more than himself, provides for her and comes home cheerfully, and the wife honors her husband greatly. He explains that each side's giving naturally draws out the other's, and that those who seek to 'liberate' the woman destroy the structure of the family.

title.en: Two heritages: the Ba'al Shem Tov and Rav Hirsch

summary.en: The Mashgiach turns to the chassan and kallah, descendants of a talmid of the Ba'al Shem Tov and of Rav Samson Raphael Hirsch, and describes what each brought: the Ba'al Shem Tov to Eastern European Jewry and Rav Hirsch to Western European Jewry. He suggests that they learn together each day from both heritages, to strengthen them against outside influences and continue both golden chains.

title.en: Rav Hirsch on Shabbos, and a brachah

summary.en: To start their learning, the Mashgiach reads a passage of Rav Hirsch describing Shabbos as the Jew's richest jewel and most loyal companion. He blesses the new couple to treasure Shabbos as their purest diamond and to fill their weekdays with avodas Hashem according to their ancestors' teachings.

catalogTitle: סומך ה'

oneLiner.en: Learning the pesukim of Ashrei from 'Somech Hashem' onward, the Mashgiach explains how Hashem raises the fallen even through a tzaddik's fall, how His hashgacha pratis provides every creature's food at its time, why one must daven for parnassa, and why no tefilah is ever lost.

abstract.en: The Mashgiach opens with the Gemara's question why Ashrei has no verse for the letter nun: it would speak of falling, and words have power, so David wrote 'Somech Hashem lechol hanoflim' instead, which the sefarim read as Hashem Himself raising Knesses Yisrael. He warns against criticizing tzaddikim: Hashem sometimes lets a tzaddik fall so he can reach and raise low souls, as the Midrash on Yosef and the brothers and the story of the Bach's sneeze show. On 'Einei chol' he contrasts the Rambam's view of hashgacha pratis with the Ba'al Shem Tov's, citing Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai and the bird, and tells stories of provision arriving exactly when needed. On 'Poseach es yadecha' he explains the duty to daven for parnassa (the Strelisker and the Ruzhiner) and tefilah as an exercise in emunah. He ends with the Ba'al Shem Tov's water carrier and the teaching that every tefilah is answered, if need be stored for later generations, as with Avraham's tefilah for Sodom.

en: David left the nun out of Ashrei because it would speak of falling, and a person's words have the power to draw down good or, chas veshalom, harm.
When a tzaddik falls it is part of Hashem's plan, so that he can go down to a low place and raise souls from there; one must not criticize tzaddikim.
According to the Ba'al Shem Tov, hashgacha pratis reaches every detail of creation, down to how a single straw falls, and every creature receives its food exactly at its time.
A Jew must ask Hashem for parnassa; tefilah is an exercise in emunah, because the very asking awakens him to recognize that Hashem is the provider.
Even when a harsh decree has been set, Hashem's attribute of mercy can sweeten and neutralize it: 'tzaddik' in His decree and 'chasid' in all His deeds.
Every tefilah is answered; when it seems unanswered it is stored in the heavenly account for later, for the person, his children or future generations.

title.en: Why Ashrei has no nun

summary.en: The Mashgiach brings the Gemara's question why there is no nun verse in Ashrei and explains that falling may not be spoken of because speech has great power. He then brings a parable from the sefarim of a king who calls back his banished queen, read into 'Somech Hashem': Hashem Himself will raise Knesses Yisrael.

title.en: When a tzaddik falls

summary.en: The Mashgiach warns against criticizing gedolei Yisrael and explains that Hashem sometimes makes a tzaddik fall so that he can repair low places. He brings Tzelafchad, a saying of Rebbe Nachman of Breslov about two mistakes people make, and the Midrash on Yosef and the brothers that 'nora alila' shows everything followed a plan.

title.en: The Bach's sneeze and Gehinom

summary.en: Discussing why the Ba'al Shem Tov did not hold stringently on chadash, the Mashgiach tells how, after the Bach's passing, no sin was found on him until an angel brought a sneeze that startled an animal and moved a wagon; Gehinom was cooled for him, and when he left he took the wicked out with him. This, he concludes, is how Hashem raises the fallen through a tzaddik.

title.en: 'Einei chol': hashgacha pratis on every creature

summary.en: On 'Einei chol eilecha yesaberu' the Mashgiach contrasts the Rambam, who limits individual hashgacha to people, with the Ba'al Shem Tov, for whom it reaches every straw, and brings the Midrash of Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai and the bird. He adds the Gemara's story of a Tanna and the young lions and explains that even a predator's prey is timed by Heaven.

title.en: Stories of provision at the right moment

summary.en: The Mashgiach tells of the Ba'al Shem Tov's thirsty disciple, who was given water by a man carrying it from a distant well for a madman poritz, and of a tzaddik who slapped his son for claiming hunger and then found a coin on the window. He concludes that Hashem shows His providence to whoever has simple emunah.

title.en: 'Poseach es yadecha': davening for parnassa

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that Ashrei is said three times a day because of 'Poseach es yadecha', and tells of the Strelisker, whose chassidim did not want parnassa, and of the Ruzhiner, who had them write it in their kvitlach. Bringing the Rambam, the Ramban and the Maharal, he explains that tefilah is an exercise in emunah and that asking for parnassa places one under Hashem's hashgacha.

title.en: Famine and plague; justice and mercy

summary.en: The Mashgiach brings the Gemara in Taanis that when there was both plague and famine one should pray for food, since whoever is given sustenance is given life, hinted in 'umasbia lechol chai'. On 'Tzaddik Hashem bechol derachav' he explains that mercy can sweeten a decree of strict justice, and raises the Gemara's contradiction whether man is judged on Rosh Hashanah or every day.

title.en: The Ba'al Shem Tov and the water carrier

summary.en: The Mashgiach tells how the Ba'al Shem Tov showed a disciple a water carrier who one day complained bitterly and the next day thanked Hashem for his health and bread. The Ba'al Shem Tov explained that the decree is set on Rosh Hashanah but the measure of mercy is judged daily, which the Mashgiach reads into 'tzaddik' and 'chasid'.

title.en: 'Karov Hashem': no tefilah is lost

summary.en: On 'Karov Hashem lechol kor'av' the Mashgiach brings Rav Hirsch on calling in truth and the principle from the sefarim that every tefilah is answered, if not now then stored in a person's heavenly account. He brings the Yetev Lev that Avraham's tefilah for Sodom was kept for later generations, and the barren women remembered together with Sarah.

catalogTitle: סוף אשרי. הללוקה הללי נפשי

oneLiner.en: The Mashgiach explains the closing verses of Ashrei and the opening of Halleluyah, Hallei Nafshi: how prayer opens Hashem's chesed beyond strict justice, how a tzaddik's praise awakens all of creation, and how a tzaddik praises Hashem with his very life.

abstract.en: The Mashgiach distinguishes Hashem's general providence, which feeds every creature according to its desire, from His particular providence, which is just in all His ways yet can be changed through prayer, since He is also kind in all His deeds. He brings the Midrash of the treasure of free gifts, opened at special times, places and through tzaddikim. On 'Hashem is close to all who call Him,' he stresses calling in truth and that no prayer is lost. 'Hashem guards all who love Him' includes those attached to a tzaddik, while one who joins a rasha suffers with him. After Ashrei, David's praise as king awakens all flesh to praise. Halleluyah, Hallei Nafshi means David joins the praise he calls for. 'I will praise Hashem with my life': a tzaddik praises Him with his whole life, even his sleep and his very existence, and should trust only in Hashem.

en: Hashem's particular providence is just in all His ways, yet because He is also kind in all His deeds, prayer can annul a decree that was justly made.
The treasure of free gifts is the greatest of all, and there are special times, places and tzaddikim through which it opens.
Every prayer said sincerely is accepted; when its answer is not seen, Hashem credits it to the person's account for later or for his children.
Those who are attached to a tzaddik are guarded together with him, and one who joins a rasha is caught up in the rasha's punishment.
A tzaddik's praise of Hashem awakens the whole creation to praise Him, each tzaddik according to his sphere of influence, and David as king awakened all of Klal Yisrael.
In 'Halleluyah, Hallei Nafshi' David first calls on others to praise and then says that his own soul praises too, since one cannot tell others to do what he does not do himself.
A tzaddik praises Hashem with his life, through everything he does, while a rasha brings honor to Heaven only through his downfall.

title.en: General and particular providence

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains 'You open Your hand' as the general providence that gives every creature what it desires, with examples of the ox, the flamingo and the cat. He then explains 'righteous in all His ways and kind in all His deeds' as the particular providence: a just decree that prayer can still annul.

title.en: The treasure of free gifts and times of favor

summary.en: The Mashgiach brings the Midrash in which Moshe Rabbeinu was shown the treasure of free gifts, the greatest of all. He lists times, places and tzaddikim through which this treasure opens, and brings the Gemara in Berachos that Hashem grants even one who is not worthy.

title.en: Calling in truth; no prayer is lost

summary.en: On 'Hashem is close to all who call Him in truth' the Mashgiach explains that prayer must be said with the mind on the words, bringing the Chovos HaLevavos' parable of the king, and that every sincere prayer is accepted even when no answer is seen. He then turns to 'He guards all who love Him' and the Gemara's teaching that the word 'es' includes what is secondary.

title.en: Joined to a tzaddik, joined to a rasha

summary.en: Following the Yismach Moshe, the Mashgiach explains that 'es kol ohavav' includes those attached to a tzaddik, and 'all the wicked He will destroy' includes those who join a rasha. He brings the king of Yehudah who was punished for joining a rasha, and Avraham, to whom Hashem spoke only after Lot left him.

title.en: A tzaddik's praise awakens all flesh

summary.en: On 'My mouth will speak Hashem's praise, and all flesh will bless,' the Mashgiach explains that a tzaddik's praise awakens all of creation, each tzaddik according to his sphere of influence, revealed or hidden. He brings the Gemara that King David ruled on questions and then asked Mefiboshes, and explains that David ruled himself because his word brought purity to all of Klal Yisrael.

title.en: After Ashrei, the urge to keep praising

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that when David finished Ashrei he was seized with longing to keep praising, and so began Halleluyah. He tells of a fiery Stoliner chassid who would say Pesukei DeZimra again with a second minyan, and of Rav Shlomo Zalman Auerbach, who would not ask others to give tzedakah without giving himself.

title.en: Praising with one's life, not one's downfall

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that 'Halleluyah' calls on others, and 'Hallei nafshi' says that David praises too; 'with my life' means putting one's whole vitality into prayer. He brings the verse that Hashem made everything for His sake, even the rasha for the day of evil, and explains that a rasha honors Heaven through his downfall, while David praises with his life.

title.en: A tzaddik is a tzaddik even in his sleep

summary.en: The Mashgiach tells how the Chiddushei HaRim and Rav Yitzchak of Vorka watched Rav Yechezkel of Kuzmir sleep, and concludes that a Rebbe is a Rebbe even asleep. He explains 'with my being' as praising even through the secondary parts of life, and 'with my life' as thanks for life itself, telling of Rav Zusha dancing because he was hungry.

title.en: Do not trust in benefactors

summary.en: On 'Do not trust in benefactors' the Mashgiach explains that only Hashem can truly help. He tells how the Chiddushei HaRim and the Vorker Rebbe considered asking Moses Montefiore to annul a Polish decree on the chadarim, and how the Chiddushei HaRim explained that one cannot rely on a person for whom the matter is not a salvation.

catalogTitle: אל תבטחו בנדיבים

oneLiner.en: Going through the chapter of Tehillim 'Al tivtechu vindivim', the Mashgiach explains that a Jew's hope rests only on Hashem, who measures every person's share of help and suffering, and that even when people help him they are only Hashem's messengers.

abstract.en: The Mashgiach opens with 'Al tivtechu vindivim': the great donors cannot be relied on, since a man can change his mind or leave the world. Yaakov Avinu is the model of bitachon; the Midrash contrasts his empty-handed journey to Charan with Eliezer's camels, and he said 'my help is from Hashem, Maker of heaven and earth'. Even when donors help, they are only messengers. Reading 'sivro' as 'shivro', the Mashgiach explains that every person's measure of suffering is fixed, so one who pours his toil into Torah and avodas Hashem is spared suffering elsewhere. He goes on through the chapter: helpers and enemies are Hashem's instruments; Hashem keeps faith across generations and gilgulim, frees trapped sparks of holiness in their time, and watches over the orphan and widow. Bitachon is drawn from Torah, tzaddikim, and the 'Tziyon' of every generation, such as Shabbos. He closes on 'Ki tov zamrah Elokeinu': Dovid HaMelech sings even under midas hadin.

en: The Mashgiach explains that one cannot rely on the donors, because a man may change his mind or leave the world, and with him his plans are lost.
Even when people do help, the one whose hope is on Hashem sees them only as a messenger; if they refuse, Hashem has another messenger.
Every person must go through suffering in this world, and how much is decreed in Heaven; nachas in one area means less in another, and suffering in one area spares another.
The Mashgiach says one should put his exertion into avodas Hashem, toiling over a Tosafos or a blatt Gemara, and thereby be spared suffering in health and in nachas from children.
Hashem's reckoning is true over many generations: a loss or an unexpected ruling may settle an account from an earlier gilgul.
Bitachon is acquired by going to the Torah and to tzaddikim and by drawing from the 'Tziyon' of each generation, in place, in soul or in time, such as Shabbos.
'Ki tov zamrah Elokeinu' teaches that Dovid HaMelech sings to Hashem even when He acts with midas hadin, since everything Hashem does is for his good.

title.en: Do not rely on the donors

summary.en: The Mashgiach observes that the largest tzedakah comes from ordinary Jews of the batei midrash, not from the rich, and reads 'al tivtechu vindivim': a man can promise, then change his mind or leave the world, and his plans are lost with him.

title.en: Yaakov, the pillar of bitachon

summary.en: On 'ashrei she'Kel Yaakov b'ezro', the Mashgiach brings the Midrash that Yaakov went to Charan with nothing, unlike Eliezer's camels, and said 'my help is from Hashem, Maker of heaven and earth'. One whose hope is on Hashem sees even helping donors as mere messengers.

title.en: Every person's measure of suffering

summary.en: Bringing a reading of 'sivro' as 'shivro', the Mashgiach explains that each person must go through a fixed measure of suffering and nachas. He tells of a man who lost a gold watch after having nachas from new curtains, and explains the custom of saying 'kaparah' over a broken glass.

title.en: Breaking oneself for Hashem

summary.en: Every person comes into the world to be broken, so the Mashgiach says one should put his toil into Torah and avodas Hashem and be spared suffering in health and children. He asks why not everyone does so and answers that they lack bitachon; one whose breaking is 'al Hashem Elokav' shows true hope.

title.en: Helpers, enemies and Hashem's true reckoning

summary.en: On 'Hashem li b'ozrai', the Mashgiach says one must thank those who help yet see Hashem behind them, and see an enemy too as Hashem's instrument, as Dovid did with Shimi ben Gera. On 'shomer emes l'olam' he explains, with Rashi, that Hashem's reckoning spans generations and gilgulim, illustrated by a din Torah before Reb Yitzchak Hamburger.

title.en: Hashem frees what is bound, in its time

summary.en: On 'Hashem matir asurim', the Mashgiach explains that Hashem arranges ways, such as bitul b'rov, for a trapped spark of holiness to become permitted. A person may not force such a release himself, just as Klal Yisrael was sworn to wait for the geulah and not take it by force.

title.en: The blind, the bent, the orphan and the widow

summary.en: The Mashgiach goes through 'pokeach ivrim', 'zokef kefufim', 'ohev tzaddikim' and 'yasom v'almanah ye'oded': those without worldly wisdom, those bent under burdens and the forsaken are not lost, for Hashem watches over them. He brings a letter of Reb Yonasan to his widowed sister that most orphans grow up successful, while the planned paths of the wicked are overturned.

title.en: Where bitachon is drawn from: Tziyon

summary.en: The Mashgiach sums up the chapter's theme as bitachon and asks where it is acquired: from the Torah, from tzaddikim and their stories, and from 'Tziyon', which today exists in soul and in time, such as Shabbos. He tells the Gemara's story of Nakdimon ben Gurion to show that Hashem's kingship of 'yimloch Hashem l'olam' is present in every generation.

title.en: Singing to Hashem even in midas hadin

summary.en: Moving to 'Ki tov zamrah Elokeinu', the Mashgiach explains that after Ashrei Dovid HaMelech could not stop praising. He contrasts mockers of long, loud davening with their own shouting at ball games, and explains that Dovid sings even under midas hadin, as in 'tzarah v'yagon emtza uvshem Hashem ekra'.

catalogTitle: Summer: Preparing for a Good Summer (Connection to שלח/קרח and תמוז/אב)

oneLiner.en: The Mashgiach explains that Tammuz and Av, the months of Reuven and Shimon that fell through Korach's machlokes and the sins of their nesi'im, hide the deepest sparks of Moshiach, so a summer journey is a shlichus from Hashem to be guarded and used.

abstract.en: The Mashgiach opens with the Zohar that Korach's machlokes was against Shabbos and Yerushalayim, the place of unity, and that Korach wanted the Middas HaDin to rule. Following Rashi, he explains that the world was first meant to be run with din and will be so in the future. Reuven, the firstborn whose stone is the red ruby, is din, so his tribe joined Korach. The months follow the order of the degalim: Tammuz belongs to Reuven and Av to Shimon, and because their nesi'im, Elitzur and Shlumiel, defiled themselves, these became months of churban, yet in the end they will turn to joy. Since the holiest sparks fall lowest, Tammuz and Av hold the most precious sparks of Moshiach. Every journey is a shlichus from Hashem, as the meraglim traveled in these months, so summer is no time for leniency: one must guard one's eyes, daven, and see Hashem in His creation.

en: Korach wanted the Middas HaDin to rule the world, and the Mashgiach explains through Rashi that the world was originally meant to be run with din and will be so in the future.
Tammuz and Av are the months of Reuven and Shimon, fourth and fifth in the degalim, and the sins of their nesi'im made them months of churban.
In the future Tammuz and Av will be restored and become the happiest months of the year, as Zechariah foretells.
Because the holiest sparks fall the lowest, Tammuz and Av hold the most precious sparks of Moshiach, and these months are a special time to work to bring him.
Wherever a person travels he is a shaliach of Hashem, and he must ask himself whether he goes as a shaliach of Hashem or of the yetzer hara.
Summer is not a time to be lenient but a time of danger and trials, when one must especially guard the eyes, since Tammuz and Av correspond to the two eyes.
In the country one can see Hashem in His creation, which sings to Him, and a Jew is meant to join that song.

title.en: Korach's machlokes and the Middas HaDin

summary.en: The Mashgiach announces ideas for the coming summer months and brings the Zohar, cited by the Chasam Sofer and the Maor VaShemesh, that Korach's machlokes was against Shabbos and Yerushalayim, the place of unity. Korach, a Levi, wanted din instead of the kehunah's chesed to be the order of the world.

title.en: The world was meant for din

summary.en: To simplify the Zohar, the Mashgiach brings Rashi at the start of Bereishis that Hashem first intended to run the world with din, and added rachamim only because the world could not stand it. In the future, he explains, the Jews will be such tzaddikim that they can live and be happy even with din.

title.en: Why Reuven joined Korach

summary.en: The Mashgiach asks why Dasan, Aviram, On and the tribe of Reuven joined Korach. He answers that Reuven, the bechor, is din, like 'reishis' and the name Elokim at creation; the firstborn lost the avodah to the Leviim after the Egel and wanted it back; and Reuven's stone on the Choshen is the red odem, called ruby or rubin, the color of pure din.

title.en: Reuven, Shimon, Tammuz and Av

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains the two orders of the shevatim: Reuven first as bechor with Shimon as his viceroy, the Choshen by birth, but in the degalim Reuven is demoted to fourth and Yehuda is first. Since the months match the shevatim of the degalim, Nissan is Yehuda's, Tammuz is Reuven's and Av is Shimon's, and Tammuz is entirely a month of din, as the Bnei Yissaschar says.

title.en: The nesi'im who brought churban

summary.en: Elitzur ben Shedeur, nasi of Reuven, joined Korach's machlokes and dragged his month, Tammuz, into churban; Shlumiel ben Tzurishaddai, nasi of Shimon, sinned and was killed by Pinchas, and Av became a month of churban. In the future both months will be restored, and as Zechariah says, their fasts will become days of joy.

title.en: Korach's tikkun and Monday's song

summary.en: The Mashgiach brings the Arizal that the last letters of 'Tzaddik katamar yifrach' spell Korach, who will come to his tikkun. Machlokes was created on Monday, the second day, when there is no 'ki tov'; therefore on Monday the song of the sons of Korach, which praises Yerushalayim, is sung.

title.en: Sparks of Moshiach in Tammuz and Av

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that Tammuz and Av are months of Moshiach: the Midrash says Moshiach is born on Tisha B'Av. Every Jew holds a spark of Moshiach, as the Meor Einayim teaches, and sparks are captive in food, drink and every place; since the holiest fall lowest, as the Tanya explains, these fallen months hold the most precious ones.

title.en: Every journey is a shlichus

summary.en: Against Elitzur and Shlumiel the Mashgiach sets Yehoshua and Kalev, whose tribes bring Moshiach ben Yosef and Moshiach ben Dovid and whose months, Tishrei and Nissan, are months of geulah. Then, with the Ba'al Shem Tov's teaching that a man's steps are set by Hashem, he explains that every trip, to Chicago or to the country, is a shlichus to raise sparks, and that the meraglim traveled in Tammuz and Av as shluchim whose intentions decided their fate.

title.en: Whose shaliach am I

summary.en: The Mashgiach says one who packs for vacation must ask whether he is a shaliach of Hashem or of the yetzer hara. Everything happens in place and time, as the law of edim zomemin shows, and Hashem sends a Jew into Tammuz and Av as a time of danger, so he must daven as Moshe davened for Yehoshua and Kalev davened for himself. He contrasts the failed meraglim with the successful shluchim of Yehoshua, who raised Rachav until she married Yehoshua.

title.en: Summer is no time for leniency

summary.en: The Mashgiach warns that a yeshiva's summer break is not a release from the winter's bonds and not a time to be lenient in tznius, kashrus or Shabbos; it is a time of danger, full of the trials of ikvesa d'Meshicha, including the electronic yetzer hara. Tammuz and Av correspond to the two eyes, so one must especially guard the eyes.

title.en: Seeing Hashem in the countryside

summary.en: The Mashgiach says the task of Tammuz and Av is to restore them, and with them Reuven, Shimon and one's own soul. In the city one sees only cement and buildings, but in the country one sees Hashem's creation, the trees, birds, streams and stars, as Yeshayahu says to lift the eyes and look.

title.en: Singing with creation, and a blessing

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains why morning is called tzafra, for the birds, and evening ramsha, for the insects, while a Jew sings by day and by night. He brings Rav Hirsch on 'Kol Hashem behadar' and tells how Rav Shraga Feivel Mendlowitz answered a man who told him to look in his siddur. He closes that a Jew must know whose shaliach he is, and blesses the listeners with a successful summer.

catalogTitle: בונה ירשלים ה'

oneLiner.en: On the words 'Boneh Yerushalayim Hashem, nidchei Yisrael yechanes', the Mashgiach teaches that every Jew is Hashem's messenger, and that the summer travels of Tammuz and Av, if made with awareness of the shlichus, gather sparks of holiness and build Yerushalayim.

abstract.en: The Mashgiach opens with the Sanzer Rav's teaching that every Jewish avodah builds the Beis Hamikdash, so that today only small things are missing, and with Dovid Hamelech's answer for why the building takes so long: Hashem is gathering the dispersed of Israel. Turning to Parshas Shelach, he brings the Chasam Sofer on the sending of the meraglim and develops the idea of shlichus: a sofer is holy only as Hashem's messenger, and every person is sent into the world on a mission, as the Sfas Emes says. A parable of a man who went to a land of diamonds and came back with spoiled tallow shows how people forget their mission. The summer travels, beginning with the forty days of the meraglim, are meant to repair their journey; the Ba'al Shem Tov teaches that Hashem sends each person where sparks await him. Galus itself serves this purpose. Tammuz and Av, the months of the eyes, call for guarding the eyes. He closes with a blessing for a healthy summer.

en: Every mitzvah and avodah of Jews builds the Beis Hamikdash; earlier generations built its great parts, and our small generation completes it with small things.
The building of Yerushalayim waits because Hashem first gathers the dispersed of Israel, as Dovid Hamelech says 'nidchei Yisrael yechanes'.
Every Jew doing a mitzvah, and every person who comes into the world, is a messenger of the Ribono shel Olam, and the holiness of his deed comes from the Sender.
The summer travels that begin with the forty days of the meraglim are meant to repair the meraglim's failed journey, but only if one remembers that he travels as Hashem's messenger.
Hashem sends each Jew to particular places, and Israel into galus, so that each soul can rectify the sparks of holiness that belong to it.
Tammuz and Av correspond to the two eyes, so guarding the eyes in these months repairs the damage of the meraglim's seeing and prepares the rebuilding of Tziyon.

title.en: The Beis Hamikdash built from small deeds

summary.en: The Mashgiach opens with Boneh Yerushalayim and tells how the Sanzer Rav said every avodah builds the Beis Hamikdash and only the paroches was missing. If so, today only small things remain, and he asks why the building takes so long, answering from 'nidchei Yisrael yechanes'.

title.en: The meraglim and the idea of shlichus

summary.en: On Parshas Shelach the Mashgiach brings the Chasam Sofer that both Hashem's command and the people's request stood behind the sending of the meraglim. He explains that the sender's power rests in the messenger: a sofer writes holiness only as Hashem's shliach, Yehoshua's spies succeeded because they went as shluchim, and the Sfas Emes says every person is Hashem's messenger.

title.en: The parable of the land of diamonds

summary.en: The Mashgiach tells a parable brought by a talmid of the Chasam Sofer: a poor man travels to a dark land whose streets are full of diamonds, but there candles are precious, so he forgets his purpose, fills his bags with tallow, and comes home with spoiled goods and only a few small diamonds.

title.en: The soul's forgotten mission

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains the parable: the soul is sent down to collect the diamonds of Torah and mitzvos but fills its bags with worldly things. He describes people running after money, and explains that the angel who fought Yaakov would not reveal his name because angels are named for their mission, and the yetzer hara wants people to forget theirs.

title.en: Summer travel and the forty days of the meraglim

summary.en: The Mashgiach notes that the meraglim set out on erev Rosh Chodesh Tammuz, and that the same season is when people go traveling. The purpose is to repair the meraglim's journey and turn Tisha B'Av into a festival, and the parsha of tzitzis that follows reminds a person, like a string tied on a finger, of his mission.

title.en: Sent to sparks that wait for us

summary.en: The Mashgiach brings the Ba'al Shem Tov on 'Me'Hashem mitz'adei gever konanu': a Jew who travels to Chicago on business is really sent to a Jew of his soul-root or to fruit holding his sparks. A tree in the country has waited thousands of years for a Jew to learn under it; vacations, rest and eating are meant to give strength to serve Hashem.

title.en: Galus to gather the sparks

summary.en: The Mashgiach brings the Yesod HaAvodah that one should always say 'it was not you who sent me here but G-d', and explains that every small act builds the Beis Hamikdash. Since Adam's sin scattered sparks across the world, Jews are sent to every land; he brings the Gemara and the Chasam Sofer on why galus is needed, and the Chasam Sofer on Rus.

title.en: Tammuz and Av, the months of the eyes

summary.en: Returning to Boneh Yerushalayim, the Mashgiach explains that Jews must be in galus to gather the sparks, and that Tammuz and Av are especially suited to building the Beis Hamikdash and will become festivals. Hidden good lies in these months like pearls on the sea floor; following the Arizal they are the two eyes, so they bring the greatest tests of the eyes.

title.en: Guarding the eyes and repairing the nesi'im

summary.en: The Mashgiach says guarding the eyes in the street is a precious avodah to rejoice in, repairing the eyes of these months toward seeing Hashem's return to Tziyon. He shows that the nesi'im of Reuven and Shimon, linked to Tammuz and Av, failed in Korach's dispute and with Zimri, and concludes that Jews travel to gather the sparks that complete Yerushalayim.

title.en: Blessing for a healthy summer

summary.en: The Mashgiach blesses the listeners with a healthy, successful summer in which they fulfil their shlichus, and explains that a Jew must eat and sleep enough to be healthy so he can learn and daven. He begins a story of a chassid of the Tzemach Tzedek who davened at length.

catalogTitle: הללוקה כי טוב זמרה

oneLiner.en: On the words 'Hallelukah ki tov zamrah', the Mashgiach explains that song belongs to the 'eighth' level above nature, which will be revealed when Moshiach builds Yerushalayim and gathers in every last scattered Jew, each one precious to Hashem like a named star.

abstract.en: The Mashgiach opens Tehillim 147 as a continuation of 'Yimloch Hashem l'olam': in the days of Moshiach the whole world will know that it is good to sing to Hashem. He brings the Berditchever Rav's saying that a chazan is a fool, since the gates of song stand beside the gates of teshuvah, and stresses how great zimrah was in the Beis Hamikdash. He then builds the idea of the number eight, which is above the seven of nature: Shavuos after the sefirah, Chanukah, milah, the eight-stringed kinor of Moshiach, Cheshvan and the third Beis Hamikdash, teshuvah, and the musical octave in which the eighth note is the first again. Moshiach will add a new note. On 'Boneh Yerushalayim Hashem, nidchei Yisrael yechanes' he links the Rambam's signs of Moshiach, Yerushalayim as the heart of the world, and the Jews as the heart of history. Every Jew is a letter in the Torah; the broken last letters will join the first. The galus lasts long because Hashem waits for every Jew, as He names every star, and His reckoning is above number.

en: The Mashgiach reads 'Hallelukah ki tov zamrah' as a continuation of 'Yimloch Hashem l'olam': in the days of Moshiach the world will recognize that singing to Hashem is good.
Eight stands for what is above the seven of nature: Chanukah, milah, Shavuos, teshuvah and the third Beis Hamikdash all belong to it.
In music the eighth note of the octave is the first again, which the Mashgiach connects to teshuvah, a return to the root; Moshiach will bring a new, eighth note.
The two halves of 'Boneh Yerushalayim Hashem, nidchei Yisrael yechanes' match the Rambam's two signs of Moshiach: building the Beis Hamikdash and gathering the exiles.
Yerushalayim is the heart of the world, and the Jewish people are the heart of all that happens in history.
The galus lasts so long because Hashem wants every scattered Jew to reach his tikkun, so that no Jew is left out.
Like the stars, which Hashem counts and calls each by name, every Jew is an individual with a name before Hashem, not a number.

candidateTopics: Yerushalayim as the heart of the world
every Jew as a letter in the Torah

title.en: Hallelukah ki tov zamrah and the power of song

summary.en: The Mashgiach opens the new chapter as a continuation of 'Yimloch Hashem l'olam', about the days of Moshiach. He brings the Berditchever Rav's saying that a chazan is a fool, since the gates of song are beside the gates of teshuvah, and describes zimrah in the Beis Hamikdash and its revival by the talmidim of the Ba'al Shem Tov.

title.en: Eight: above the seven of nature

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that seven stands for the middos and the world of nature, and eight for what is above it. He brings Shavuos after the sefirah, the Maharal on Chanukah, milah on the eighth day, the Gemara in Arachin on the kinor of eight strings in the days of Moshiach, the Bnei Yissaschar on Cheshvan and the third Beis Hamikdash, and teshuvah, which preceded the world.

title.en: The octave, teshuvah and the new note of Moshiach

summary.en: The Mashgiach says much wisdom of music came from the Jews, and shows that in the octave the eighth note is the first again. This explains the Berditchever's words, and why in the days of Moshiach, the 'eighth', a new note will be added and it will be good to sing to Hashem.

title.en: Boneh Yerushalayim and the signs of Moshiach

summary.en: On 'Boneh Yerushalayim Hashem, nidchei Yisrael yechanes' the Mashgiach brings the Rambam's two signs of Moshiach, building the Beis Hamikdash and gathering the exiles, and calls this the return of yovel and of teshuvah. He then begins to explain that Yerushalayim is the heart of the world.

title.en: Yerushalayim and the Jews: the heart of the world

summary.en: The Mashgiach shows from the Zohar, the Kuzari and history that everything revolves around Eretz Yisrael and Yerushalayim, from the news to the wars and the world's religions, and that the turning point against Rommel came at its border. Everything in the world happens for the sake of the Jews, as the Nazi leader's obsession with killing the Jews of Hungary at the cost of the war shows.

title.en: From beis to lamed: the broken heart made whole

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that every Jew is a letter in the Torah: the great souls are the beis of Bereishis and the last generations are the last letters, with the broken lamed. When the Torah is read as a circle, as on Simchas Torah, the lamed meets the beis; so Moshiach, the soul of Moshe, will join the broken Jews to the first, and this is 'Harofei lishvurei lev'.

title.en: Why the galus lasts so long

summary.en: Returning to the passuk, the Mashgiach says that then one will sing even about the middas hadin of the galus. He asks why the galus lasts so long and answers that Hashem waits for every scattered Jew to reach his tikkun, and tells of a tzaddik who would not bring Moshiach at the cost of losing such Jews.

title.en: Moneh mispar lakochavim: a name, not a number

summary.en: The Mashgiach compares a Jew who seems to be nothing to a newly found star many times larger than the earth. On 'Moneh mispar lakochavim, lechulam shemos yikra' he explains the difference between a number and a name, with the cattle herd, children, the Nazis' tattooed numbers and the counting 'b'mispar shemos', and says every creation and every Jew has a function no other can fill.

title.en: Lisvunaso ein mispar: Hashem's reckoning above number

summary.en: The Mashgiach asks how a Jew who shows no Jewishness can hold up the geulah, and answers with 'Gadol Adoneinu… lisvunaso ein mispar': Hashem's understanding does not work with numbers. Tzion is above the laws of mathematics, as the Aron took up no space and the crowded Azarah had room for all, and so one must wait for 'Boneh Yerushalayim'.

catalogTitle: מונה מספר לכוכבים

oneLiner.en: Going through the psalm of Hallelukah ki tov zamrah, the Mashgiach explains that Hashem counts and names every Jew like the stars, that every creature has its own mission, and that the hardships of exile are a preparation for the song of the days of Moshiach.

abstract.en: Returning to the verse 'He counts the number of the stars, He calls them all by name', the Mashgiach explains that every Jew, even the broken and forgotten, has a name, and a name is a mission. He digresses to Adam naming Chava after the curse, and tells how a Rebbe declined to name a child for its father. A name change for a sick person gives him a new mission. People who seem small and unlucky are like the stars, which only look small. From Gadol Adoneinu and me'oded anavim he teaches that every person contributes to the world. When Moshiach comes, a new song will reveal the purpose of exile, which is like clouds and rain that make things grow. Hashem feeds even the raven's young, and the ravens fed Eliyahu, a soul of the days of Moshiach. Hashem desires those who hope for Him, not the strength of horses. Even decrees in exile are softened, like snow that falls as wool.

en: Every Jew has a name and not a number, and his name is his particular mission in the world.
People who seem insignificant are like the stars, which look small but are enormous, and every creature, down to a caterpillar, has a mission without which the world would not be complete.
When Moshiach comes a new song will be sung, because then it will be seen what the exile and the small, forgotten people accomplished.
The exile is like a dreary, rainy day whose clouds and rain prepare the growth of a spring that will come with the redemption.
Hashem desires not physical might but those who fear Him and hope for His kindness every day.
Even in exile Hashem softens harsh decrees, as snow comes down like wool and is scattered like dust.

title.en: A name is a mission; Adam names Chava

summary.en: The Mashgiach returns to the verse about Hashem naming the stars: every Jew has a name, and a name is a mission, as the Arizal and Rashi show. In a digression he explains how Adam, instead of blaming Chava after the curses, named her 'mother of all life', and Hashem in turn clothed them.

title.en: Names, illness, and the unseen greatness of the small

summary.en: The Mashgiach tells how the Chiddushei HaRim refused to choose a child's name for its father, explains that a name change can give a sick person a new mission, and compares people whose lives seem failed to the stars, which only look small. Every creature, even a caterpillar, is a needed part of the great machine of creation.

title.en: Gadol Adoneinu: encouragement for the humble

summary.en: From 'Great is our Lord, His understanding is beyond number' the Mashgiach explains that every person does something good for the world, even the worst rasha who once did a mitzvah. 'Hashem encourages the humble' is a chizuk for small people, while the oppressors who build themselves on others are brought low.

title.en: The new song of Moshiach and the clouds of exile

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that these psalms speak of the coming of Moshiach, when a new song will be sung for everything not understood before. The exile, with its questions, is like a dark rainy day; 'He covers the heavens with clouds' to prepare the rain that makes the spring bloom.

title.en: Singing now; Hashem feeds the raven's young

summary.en: The Mashgiach says Dovid HaMelech calls on a person to sing to Hashem already now, with the abilities he has. 'He gives the animal its bread, to the young ravens' shows that every creature counts: Hashem feeds the raven's chicks though the raven, which lacked mercy in the ark, abandons them. The ravens that fed Eliyahu show that in the days of Moshiach the raven will become merciful.

title.en: Not the strength of the horse, but those who hope

summary.en: On 'Not in the strength of the horse does He desire', the Mashgiach contrasts the nations' pride in might, which he ties to the Greek culture of sport fought on Chanukah, with what Hashem wants. Hashem desires those who fear Him and hope every day for Moshiach, as the Rambam counts among the principles of faith.

title.en: Praise, Yerushalayim, and the swift redemption

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains 'Praise Hashem, Yerushalayim' as addressed to the Jewish people even while the city lies in ruins, promising strengthened gates, peaceful borders and the finest wheat. To the question how to praise for a hope not yet fulfilled, he answers from 'He sends His word to the earth, swiftly runs His word': when the time comes, the redemption comes at once, as seen in the Megillah.

title.en: Snow like wool: the decree softened

summary.en: On 'He gives snow like wool', the Mashgiach explains that Hashem gives the cold of exile according to the warmth a person has, and when Jews daven strongly a decree that cannot be undone is crushed to powder, like the mashal of the king who had the stone ground before it was thrown at his son. Snow is middas hadin, yet Hashem sweetens it with mercy, and Jews survive the exile.

catalogTitle: ט”ו בשבט: Tu Bishvat, Moshiach and Birthdays

oneLiner.en: The Mashgiach explains why the Mishnah on Tu Bishvat gives Beis Shammai's view first, learns from it that a Jew who truly expects Moshiach acts on it, and teaches that a person's real birthday is the day he fulfills his mission.

abstract.en: The Mashgiach opens with the Mishnah of the four Rosh Hashanahs and notes its unusual wording: instead of listing Beis Shammai and Beis Hillel side by side, it states the first of Shevat as the Rosh Hashanah for trees, as if ruling like Beis Shammai, and only then gives the fifteenth. The date decides which year fruit belongs to for terumah and maaser. Since there is a tradition that when Moshiach comes the halacha will follow Beis Shammai, a pious Jew goes out twice, on Rosh Chodesh Shevat and on Tu Bishvat; both views are real to him. From this the Mashgiach learns what it means to be conscious of Moshiach, crediting the Lubavitcher Rebbe with making the world expect him. Turning to birthdays, he reads Pharaoh's birthday in Bereishis as the day he was born for his mission, and says each day carries such a mission.

en: The Mashgiach explains that Rosh Hashanah for trees decides which year a tree's fruit belongs to for terumah and maaser, so the owner marks which trees have blossomed.
Because the halacha will follow Beis Shammai when Moshiach comes, the Mashgiach says a pious Jew marks his trees both on Rosh Chodesh Shevat and on Tu Bishvat.
The Mashgiach credits the Lubavitcher Rebbe with making the Jewish world conscious of Moshiach and expecting him every moment.
According to the Mashgiach, a person's real birthday is the day he accomplishes the mission for which he was sent into the world.
The Mashgiach says every day and every moment carries a mission, so each day can be a birthday.

a person's mission in the world

title.en: The Mishnah's unusual wording on Tu Bishvat

summary.en: The Mashgiach brings the Mishnah of the four Rosh Hashanahs and asks why it states the first of Shevat as if ruling like Beis Shammai, instead of the usual form. He explains the halacha that terumah and maaser must be taken from fruit of the same year.

title.en: Marking the trees twice

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that the owner of a grove marks which trees have blossomed by Tu Bishvat, and that a pious Jew, mindful of the tradition that the halacha will follow Beis Shammai when Moshiach comes, marks them on Rosh Chodesh Shevat as well. This answers the Mishnah's wording: both opinions are relevant to us.

title.en: Living with Moshiach

summary.en: The Mashgiach learns from the Mishnah that a Jew who truly believes in Moshiach expects him this year and acts on it. He addresses the Lubavitcher chassidim present and says the Lubavitcher Rebbe made the world conscious of Moshiach.

title.en: Pharaoh's birthday and the true birthday

summary.en: Turning to those celebrating a birthday, the Mashgiach reads the Torah's phrase for Pharaoh's birthday as the day he was caused to be born, the day of his mission to free Yosef. He concludes that a person's real birthday is when he fulfills his mission, that every day carries a mission, and closes with a brachah.

catalogTitle: משליך קרחו כפתים

oneLiner.en: Through the closing verses of Tehillim 147, the Mashgiach shows how Hashem sweetens His din, how rain and snow are rooted in chesed and carry Torah, and how a Jew keeps the chok with simple emunah until he is granted to understand it.

abstract.en: The Mashgiach continues with the verse 'He casts His ice like crumbs'. Nissan and the summer are a time of chesed, of warmth and expansion; Tishrei and the winter are din and contraction, and from the cold comes ice. Yet Hashem sweetens the din: the ice falls as flakes, and the snow is white, the color of chesed, like milk and the manna, food given without toil. Then 'He sends His word and melts them': snow is frozen water, and water is chesed. The rain carries blessing and, inwardly, Torah. The Mashgiach brings the Zohar that Noach could have received the Torah and returned as Moshe, and explains Matan Torah as a 'mabul' of Torah. On 'His chukim and mishpatim to Yisrael' he describes the Akeidah: Avraham went with emunah shleimah without understanding, and only afterward understood. He closes with Tehillim 148 and man's role in leading all creation in praise.

en: The summer months from Nissan are a time of chesed, warmth and expansion, while the winter months from Tishrei are din, cold and contraction.
Hashem sweetens the din of winter: the ice comes down as flakes and the snow is white, the color of chesed, like milk and the manna, which are food given freely.
The root of snow is water, which is chesed; when Hashem melts it, the rain brings blessing, and the inner soul of rain is Torah.
At Matan Torah the heavens showed the sign of a mabul, but instead of a flood of water there came down a flood of Torah.
Avraham went to the Akeidah with emunah shleimah, without understanding how Hashem's promise about Yitzchak would be kept, and the test of emunah is to believe even with questions.
First comes the chok, kept without understanding, and afterward the mishpat, when Hashem grants understanding to those who keep the Torah.
Man, and the Jew in particular, holds the control of all creation, so that the angels' praise depends on the praise of the Jews.

the soul of rain is Torah
Matan Torah as a flood of Torah

title.en: Months of chesed and months of din

summary.en: Returning to 'He casts His ice like crumbs', the Mashgiach explains that from Nissan begins a rule of chesed, shown in the straight order of the letters of 'aviv', while Tishrei is din, its letters in reverse. Summer is warmth and expansion, winter is cold and contraction, and from that din comes the ice.

title.en: Why the snow is white

summary.en: The Mashgiach asks why Hashem sends the ice as flakes and answers that He sweetens the din with rachamim. The whiteness of the snow is chesed, like milk, the food of infants who are exempt from toiling for bread, and like the white manna of the generation of the desert; then a thaw gives people and animals relief.

title.en: The thaw, the rain and its soul

summary.en: On 'He sends His word and melts them', the Mashgiach explains that the root of snow is water, which is chesed, held back in winter and released by Hashem's wind. Rain brings great blessing, as the Gemara in Taanis says, and since every physical thing has a soul, the soul of rain is Torah.

title.en: Noach, Moshe and a mabul of Torah

summary.en: The Mashgiach brings the Zohar that the Torah could have been given through Noach, and that Noach's soul returned as Moshe, which explains the Gemara's hint of Moshe in 'beshagam' and why the flood is called 'the waters of Noach'. He then explains the nations' fear of a flood at Matan Torah: it was a flood of Torah, and the letter shin turns 'mabul' into 'b'shalom'.

title.en: The rainy season and 'maggid'

summary.en: The Mashgiach says a rainy day brings down an influence of Torah, so the rainy season, when one asks for rain for blessing, is a time to merit Torah. He explains 'maggid' as drawing forth, like the gidim that carry blood to the limbs: through the rain Hashem channels His word to Yaakov.

title.en: The Akeidah: emunah without understanding

summary.en: The Mashgiach describes the test of the Akeidah: Hashem had promised that the nation would come from Yitzchak, who had no children, and now commanded to offer him. Avraham did not understand, yet went with emunah shleimah, leaving the 'how' to Hashem; many failed this test in the Holocaust, and the Mashgiach answers with the mashal of a tailor cutting silk.

title.en: First the chok, then the mishpat

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that one who keeps the mitzvos without understanding is afterward granted understanding, while one who demands reasons first is never shown the sweetness of Shabbos or of learning. This is 'His chukim and mishpatim to Yisrael': first a chok, then a mishpat, as Avraham understood the Akeidah only afterward; the nations do not know even the mishpatim.

title.en: Man leads creation in praise

summary.en: Beginning Tehillim 148, the Mashgiach explains that man was given control over the upper and lower worlds, a control that passed to Avraham and the Jews, so that the angels praise only after the Jews do. Man is the living soul of creation, and David HaMelech calls on heaven and earth to sing together; 'shamayim' means the remote 'there', and 'meromim' a height beyond grasp.

catalogTitle: הללוקה הללו את ה' מן השמים

oneLiner.en: Going through Tehillim 148 and the opening of 149, the Mashgiach explains that all of creation sings to Hashem by doing His will, but the praise of man, who has free choice, is the greater one, and that in the days of Moshiach the honest Jews who praise Hashem now in disgrace will be honored.

abstract.en: The Mashgiach explains Tehillim 148 verse by verse. David HaMelech, as the soul of Adam and the key of creation, commands the heavens, the angels, the sun and moon and the higher heavens to praise Hashem, because through the service of the tzaddik all of creation sings. Their song is simply doing Hashem's will, as in Perek Shirah, since they were created by His command and have no free choice. He then turns to the earth: the sea creatures, fire and hail, and the storm wind, which even as the harshest klipah does Hashem's word, so that every bullet has an address. Domem, tzomeach, chai and medaber, and even kings, are like puppets on strings. Men have free choice; the wicked who carry out a decree are punished because they volunteered. Therefore the praise of earth comes before heaven, and in the days of Moshiach the chassidim, now mocked, will be honored and a new song with an eighth note will be sung.

en: David HaMelech, as the soul of Adam and the key of creation, can command all of creation to praise Hashem, because the service of the tzaddik is what causes the whole creation to sing.
The song of every creation is the very fact that it does Hashem's will: a caterpillar climbing a tree or a flowing stream is singing its shirah.
The heavenly hosts have no free choice; they function by a fixed law, 'chok nasan velo ya'avor', while man in the lower world has free choice.
Even the most harmful forces, the storm wind and the kings of the earth, can do nothing except as Hashem commands; every bullet has an address.
Because men praise Hashem out of free choice, the earth is mentioned before the heavens in 'hodo al eretz veshamayim'.
In exile honest Jews are mocked and called crazy, but when Moshiach comes they will be honored, and a new song will be sung to Hashem.

candidateTopics: free will and praise of Hashem
honor of the righteous in the days of Moshiach

title.en: David calls on the heavens to praise

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that David HaMelech, the soul of Adam and the key of creation, commands the heavens, the angels, the sun and moon and the higher heavens to praise Hashem. He brings the Rambam that the heavenly bodies have intellect and sing, and explains that it is the tzaddik's service that causes creation to sing.

title.en: The song of creation is doing His will

summary.en: On 'ki hu tzivah venivra'u' the Mashgiach explains that the shirah of every creature, as in Perek Shirah, is that it does Hashem's will, from the sun Yehoshua stopped to a caterpillar and a stream. The heavenly hosts were set by a law they cannot transgress and have no free choice, unlike our world.

title.en: Praise from the earth and the storm wind

summary.en: David turns to the earth: the sea creatures, fire and hail, snow and the storm wind. The Mashgiach explains the four klipos of Yechezkel's vision, of which the storm wind is the worst, and shows that even it does Hashem's word and can harm only with His permission, so that every bullet has an address.

title.en: Four levels of creation and the kings

summary.en: The Mashgiach shows that the verses follow the four levels of domem, tzomeach, chai and medaber, ending with the kings, princes and judges of the earth, who are like puppets on strings in Hashem's hand. He then reads 'bachurim vegam besulos' with the Sefer Chassidim, illustrated with a story about strawberries with cream.

title.en: Free choice makes man's praise greater

summary.en: Men have free choice, yet Hashem's will is done regardless; the wicked who serve as His agents are punished because they volunteered, as the Rambam discusses about Pharaoh. Because men can choose not to praise, their praise shows that Hashem's name alone is exalted, and so earth comes before heaven in the verse.

title.en: The honor of Klal Yisrael in Moshiach's days

summary.en: On 'vayarem keren le'amo, tehilah lechol chasidav' the Mashgiach explains that in the days of Moshiach it will be revealed that the Jews were always the center of creation and the conductors of its song. Today Jews are disgraced among the nations and the chassidim among the Jews, and this is what we pray for on Rosh Hashanah.

title.en: Called crazy: the honest Jew in exile

summary.en: The Mashgiach brings the Gemara on the time before Moshiach, that one who turns from evil is considered mad, the Lechovitcher's blessing to his chassidim that they be called crazy, and the story of a refugee in Detroit whose uncle called him crazy for not working on Shabbos. When Moshiach comes it will be clear who is really crazy.

title.en: A new song for the time of Moshiach

summary.en: On 'shiru laHashem shir chadash, tehilaso bikhal chasidim' the Mashgiach brings the Midrash that the angels will say kadosh before the tzaddikim, so a new song will be needed for Hashem. He brings the Rambam and the Yerushalmi that simple Jews will then have perceptions greater than prophets, and describes the new song as music with an eighth note.

catalogTitle: הללוקה שירו לה' שיר חדש

oneLiner.en: Learning Tehillim 149, the Mashgiach explains the 'new song' of the time of Moshiach, when the joy of Hashem and of Klal Yisrael will be complete for the first time, the hard times of galus will be seen as kindness, and the chassidim will sing in perfect bitachon.

abstract.en: The Mashgiach learns Tehillim 149 verse by verse. A new world order will need a new song, sung above all by the chassidim, as at the Simchas Beis HaSho'eivah. Though the world looks worse, it grows better each year; every Chanukah brings down a greater light, and the new grain is permitted only after Pesach, the festival of redemption. 'Yismach Yisrael b'osav' teaches that until Moshiach neither Hashem nor any person has had complete joy; Shlomo HaMelech alone, at the dedication of the Beis HaMikdash, a foretaste of Moshiach, fulfilled all his desires. At the end of days the tzaddikim will dance in a circle, and the drum of galus will be praised together with the harp. Yosef's suffering proved to be for his good. 'Yerannenu al mishkevosam' is bitachon, shown by Chizkiyahu and Yaakov Avinu, opposed by Pharaoh; Kislev is the month of bitachon.

en: In the time of Moshiach a new era will be revealed, and the present forms of song will not suffice; a new song on new instruments will be needed to praise Hashem for it.
Although the world appears to grow worse, it is in truth getting better each year, coming closer to its tikkun; every Shabbos and every Chanukah is greater than the one before.
Until Moshiach comes there has been no complete joy, neither for Hashem with His creation nor for any person, who never fully attains his aspirations.
When Moshiach comes, the blows of galus, like the beating of a drum, will be recognized as Hashem's kindness and praised together with the sweet sounds of the harp.
'Yerannenu al mishkevosam' describes bitachon: a person at peace with Hashem can sleep, while one who lacks something lies awake in fear.
Kislev is the month of bitachon; it is a time for a Jew to gird himself with trust in Hashem, as the Chashmonaim did.

Chanukah as the light of Moshiach

title.en: A new song for a new world

summary.en: The Mashgiach opens Tehillim 149 and explains that a new era will need new forms of song, sung chiefly by the chassidim, as at the Simchas Beis HaSho'eivah. He adds that the world, though it looks worse, grows better each year, and that every Chanukah brings down a new light.

title.en: Chanukah's light and the new grain

summary.en: The Mashgiach shows that Chanukah's greatness was revealed only in later generations, being the light of Moshiach, and that each year the yomim tovim grow brighter. Through the sparks of holiness in bread he explains why the new grain is permitted only once Pesach, the festival of redemption, arrives.

title.en: Yismach Yisrael b'osav

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains the plural 'osav' as a term of majesty, and brings that at every Jewish simcha the souls of the ancestors come down, with an episode from the Skverer Rebbe's wedding. From the Midrash on 'yismach' he concludes that neither Hashem nor Klal Yisrael has yet had complete joy; it will come with Moshiach.

title.en: Shlomo HaMelech's day of complete joy

summary.en: The Mashgiach asks why no person ever fulfills all his ambitions, and answers that one cannot be better off than Hashem, whose joy in creation is not yet complete. The one exception was Shlomo HaMelech at the dedication of the Beis HaMikdash, the full moon fifteen generations from Avraham and a sample of Moshiach, which is why the Haftarah of Shemini Atzeres ends with his fulfilled desire.

title.en: The circle dance, the drum and the harp

summary.en: After noting the small meal of Shemini Atzeres and Simchas Torah, the Mashgiach explains 'yehallelu shemo vemachol': with Moshiach the tzaddikim will dance in a circle, all equal, as the Gemara at the end of Taanis describes. He contrasts the drum's beating with the harp's sweetness, and says the blows of galus will then be praised as Hashem's kindness.

title.en: Ki rotzeh Hashem b'amo: Yosef appeased

summary.en: The Mashgiach brings the Midrash linking 'vayritzuhu min habor' to 'ki rotzeh Hashem b'amo': when Yosef left prison he saw that all his suffering had been for his good. So too Hashem will appease His people, and 'yefaer anavim bishuah' means He will crown the downtrodden of galus with salvation.

title.en: Singing on their beds: bitachon and sleep

summary.en: On 'ya'lzu chasidim bechavod, yerannenu al mishkevosam' the Mashgiach explains that the worried cannot sleep while one with bitachon sleeps in peace. He brings the Midrash on Chizkiyahu, who slept the night Sancheirev besieged Yerushalayim, and Yaakov Avinu, who laid the stones of the mizbe'ach around his head as protection and slept.

title.en: Pharaoh's sleep and Kislev, month of bitachon

summary.en: The Mashgiach says emunah comes from Avraham and bitachon from Yaakov, and contrasts Pharaoh, who went to sleep on the night of the plague of the firstborn, which Hashem arranged to strengthen the bitachon of the Jews. He closes with Kislev, named for bitachon and linked to sleep in Sefer Yetzirah, as a time to serve Hashem with trust as the Chashmonaim did.

catalogTitle: Ocean Waves: The Striving of the Rising Waves

oneLiner.en: The Mashgiach explains that ocean waves are the lower waters straining to rise toward Hashem, and tells the bochurim that unlike the waves, a Jew who strives to rise in Torah will get there.

abstract.en: The Mashgiach praises the bochurim who devote themselves to Torah and avodas Hashem despite today's temptations, saying the Shechinah has nachas from them. He shares a thought from that morning, when he watched the sunrise over the ocean and the high waves crashing on the sand. Why does the sea have waves? Physics is not the final answer, since Hashem made its laws for a reason. At creation the waters were separated into upper and lower waters, and the lower waters weep, wanting to be near the King. Nisuch hamayim gave them a way to serve Hashem; since the Churban they weep again, and the Yismach Moshe reads the weeping by the rivers of Babylon in this light. The waves are the waters trying to rise; they never succeed, yet Hashem praises their effort. A Jew is different: if he yearns and struggles, he will get there. The Mashgiach closes with 'ashreichem'.

en: The Shechinah has nachas from bochurim who devote themselves to Torah and avodas Hashem despite the temptations of the time.
The laws of physics that make waves were themselves created by Hashem for a spiritual reason.
The lower waters, separated from the upper waters at creation, weep because they want to be near the King.
The waves are the lower waters trying to rise; they cannot succeed, yet Hashem praises them for trying.
Unlike the waves, a Jew who yearns and struggles to rise in Torah will get there.

title.en: Praise for the bochurim; sunrise over the ocean

summary.en: The Mashgiach praises the bochurim who devote themselves to Torah despite today's temptations and says the Shechinah has nachas from them. Pressed for time, he shares a thought from that morning, when he watched the sunrise over the ocean and the high waves crashing on the sand.

title.en: Why the waves rise: the weeping lower waters

summary.en: The Mashgiach asks why the sea has waves and answers from the separation of the waters at creation: the lower waters weep to be near the King. He brings nisuch hamayim, the Churban, the Yismach Moshe on the rivers of Babylon, and the passuk in Tehillim that Hashem praises the rising waves for trying, though they can never reach.

title.en: A Jew who strives will get there

summary.en: The Mashgiach tells the bochurim they are not like the waves: a Jew who yearns and struggles to rise in Torah will reach his goal, as many who found learning hard when young did. He closes with 'ashreichem' and the assurance that they will bring nachas ruach to the Shechinah.

catalogTitle: הללוקה הללו קל בקדשו

oneLiner.en: The Mashgiach explains the closing verses of Tehillim 149 and the whole of Tehillim 150, showing how every voice, every instrument and finally the silent neshama join in the praise of Hashem that will be complete when Moshiach comes.

abstract.en: The Mashgiach continues Tehillim 149: the chassidim carry the praises of Hashem in their throat as a double-edged sword, praising Him even before the salvation comes. The revenge on the nations at the end of days will be the truth itself, when they see that the whole exile was for the good of the Jews, just as Yosef's brothers discovered that the 'ruler of the land' was their brother. From the hadar of the chassidim he turns to the eighth king, Hadar, as a hint to the eighth world of Moshiach. He then shows how Tehillim is framed by Tehilla leDavid and the closing Halleluka chapters, and explains Tehillim 150 verse by verse: praise as union with Hashem, praise for gevurah as for chesed, the shofar and the sweet instruments, the drum that keeps the rhythm, and finally the neshama, the silent instrument that gives life to all the songs.

en: The praises of Hashem in the mouth of the chassidim are their double-edged sword, with which they overcome every obstacle and enemy.

The vengeance on the nations in the days of Moshiach will be the revealed truth that the entire exile was for the good of the Jews, as Yosef's brothers discovered the 'harsh ruler' was their loving brother.
The eighth king of Edom, Hadar, alludes to the 'eighth world' of Moshiach, which is above the seven days of creation and has no death.
Halleluka is one word because a Jew who praises Hashem should cleave to Him until he is nullified like a candle before a torch.
One praises Hashem for His gevurah and judgment just as for His chesed.
After all the instruments comes the neshama, the silent instrument that is not heard yet gives the breath of life to all the songs of praise.

candidateTopics: end of exile and the revealed truth
Yosef revealing himself to his brothers
the eighth king Hadar and the world of Moshiach

title.en: Praise as a double-edged sword

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains 'romemos Kel bigronam' as the chassidim praising Hashem even before their salvation, and calls this praise the double-edged sword that defeats every enemy. He then reads 'la'asos nekama bagoyim' as the revenge of the truth revealed at the end of days.

title.en: Yosef and his brothers: the exile turned around

summary.en: The Mashgiach compares the end of exile to Yosef revealing himself: the brothers thought the ruler of Egypt was their enemy, and with the words 'ani Yosef' everything turned around. So the nations will see that the whole exile was for Israel's good, and that truth will be their shame and their punishment, 'mishpat kasuv' and 'hadar' for the chassidim.

title.en: The eighth king, Hadar, and the eighth world

summary.en: The Mashgiach brings the parsha of the kings of Edom at the end of Vayishlach: seven kings reigned and died, but of the eighth, Hadar, no death is written. Hadar hints at the eighth world of Moshiach; he connects it to the esrog of Sukkos and Shemini Atzeres, to the eighth day of Chanukah and to Pharaoh's interpreters who could reach only seven.

title.en: Tehillim's close and the one word Halleluka

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that Tehilla leDavid is the crown of Tehillim, after which David asks all flesh to join his praise, opening the Halleluka chapters. He then explains that Halleluka is one word because the one who praises must become one with Hashem, nullified like a candle before a torch.

title.en: Praise below and above; gevurah and gedulah

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that praise in the Beis Hamikdash and the shul gives the angels the power to praise in heaven. He explains why chesed is called gedulah (it spreads outward) and gevurah is contraction, and says one praises Hashem for His judgment just as for His kindness.

title.en: The instruments of praise

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains the instruments of Tehillim 150: the shofar that brings fear, the sweet nevel and kinor, the drum that keeps the rhythm of the dance, and the cymbals. Even the noise of the drum is part of the symphony of Hashem's guidance of the world, and in the days of Moshiach every Jewish soul will reach its tikkun and join this praise.

title.en: David signs his name: Adam, David, Moshiach

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that 'kol haneshama' is David's signature at the end of Tehillim: Adam, who included all souls, came again as David and will come as Moshiach. He then returns to the frame: after Tehilla leDavid David asks everyone to join, and 'Halleluka ki tov zamra' tells how sweet praise is, as anyone who has had a good davening knows.

title.en: From all creation to a new song to the neshama

summary.en: The Mashgiach traces the last chapters: in 148 all creation, even the stormy wind of the klipah, praises; in 149 every creature should add a new song, quality rather than quantity; in 150 come all the instruments. Last comes the neshama, the inaudible instrument that gives life to all the praise, and he says one must praise with the whole soul and with hislahavus.

catalogTitle: שיר המעלות אל ה' בצרתה לי

oneLiner.en: Learning the first two Shir Hamaalos (Tehillim 120 and 121), the Mashgiach explains that the galus is a climb up to Yerushalayim, that a Jew must pray for the Shechinah's pain and guard his mouth from every trace of falsehood, and that when no help remains in this world, help comes from above nature.

abstract.en: Having finished Pesukei d'Zimra, the Mashgiach turns to the fifteen Shir Hamaalos, which the Gemara links to David HaMelech's digging of the foundations of the mizbe'ach and to the fifteen steps on which the Levi'im sang; they form an ascent from galus to the Beis HaMikdash. On 'el Hashem batzarasa li' he explains that the troubles of galus are steps upward, and brings the Bnei Yissaschar, based on the Ba'al Shem Tov, that one should pray for the Shechinah, which suffers in every Jewish pain. A parable about animals blaming a sheep shows how the world blames all Jews for one Jew's sin. He then explains 'sfas sheker' and 'lashon remiya', the holiness and power of the mouth, Meshech and Kedar, and the enemies who talk peace and mean war. On Tehillim 121 he teaches that help comes 'me'ayin', from above nature, when nothing else is left, illustrated by a story of the Ruzhiner, and closes with the Midrash on Yaakov Avinu robbed by Eliphaz.

en: The fifteen Shir Hamaalos are a sequence of ascent: the whole galus is a march up to Yerushalayim, and its troubles are steps toward the Beis HaMikdash.

Following the Bnei Yissaschar based on the Ba'al Shem Tov, the Mashgiach teaches that in every pain of a Jew the Shechinah suffers with him, so one should pray for the Shechinah and then he too is helped.
'Sfas sheker' means even the edge of falsehood and 'lashon remiya' is deceit dressed up as kosher; the Mashgiach says one must keep far even from the border of a lie.
Speech is what raises man above the animals; one who guards his mouth has great power in tefillah, while a mouth that is misused loses its power and makes a person worse than an animal.
The Mashgiach reads 'me'ayin yavo ezri' as help that comes from 'nothing', from above nature: when a Jew sees there is no help left in this world, then Hashem's help comes.
The mountains to which one raises his eyes are the powers of this world, which cannot help; help is only from Hashem, Maker of heaven and earth, who is higher than them.
