reliance on Hashem rather than the nations

title.en: The fifteen Shir Hamaalos as an ascent

summary.en: After finishing Pesukei d'Zimra the Mashgiach turns to the Shir Hamaalos, some of which are said on Shabbos. He brings the Gemara that David HaMelech said them when the waters rose from the foundations of the mizbe'ach, and that they correspond to the fifteen steps where the Levi'im sang, forming a sequence of ascent to the Beis HaMikdash.

title.en: Troubles of galus as steps upward

summary.en: On 'el Hashem batzarasa li karasi vaya'aneni' the Mashgiach explains that galus is a march to Yerushalayim and its troubles are stepping stones. He brings the Bnei Yissaschar, based on the Ba'al Shem Tov, that the Shechinah shares every Jewish pain, so one should pray for the Shechinah, and notes how low the honor of Klal Yisrael has fallen today.

title.en: The parable of the sheep and the straw

summary.en: The Mashgiach tells a humorous reading of the last passuk of Tehillim 119: in a plague among the animals the judges acquit the tiger and the wolf but convict the sheep that ate straw from a shoe. He applies it to the world, which excuses every sin of the nations but blames all Jews for the sin of one, and says the honor of Heaven has fallen very low.

title.en: Sfas sheker and lashon remiya

summary.en: The Mashgiach says that a prayer for the Shechinah is answered only when it is sincere, and explains the next passuk: 'sfas sheker' is even the edge of a lie and 'lashon remiya' is deceit made to look kosher. He brings 'midvar sheker tirchak' and the Midrash that Hashem set guards on the mouth, and that Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai wished man had two mouths.

title.en: The holiness and power of the mouth

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that one who guards his holy mouth has great power, so that his word is fulfilled and his tefillos answered, while a defiled mouth loses its power. Speech, the 'ruach memalela' given to Adam, is man's whole advantage over animals, so one who misuses it is worse than them.

title.en: Arrows of a warrior, and Meshech

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains 'chitzei gibor shenunim im gachalei resamim': bad speech harms from far away like arrows, and lasts a long time like the coals of the broom tree. He then explains 'oya li ki garti meshech', identifying Meshech with the wild people of Russia.

title.en: Kedar and those who hate peace

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that Kedar are the Arabs, whom the Rambam calls the greatest liars, and that worse than dwelling with them is dwelling with a deceitful Jew. On 'ani shalom vechi adaber hemah lamilchamah' he describes leaders who speak peace to the Jews and war to their own people, and says David HaMelech is speaking of our times.

title.en: Shir lamaalos: help from 'ayin'

summary.en: The Mashgiach notes that Tehillim 121 alone says 'shir lamaalos': it is a song to Hashem who goes with a Jew and lifts him up the steps. The mountains are the world's powers on which people rely, but help is only from Hashem; and through a Midrash on the word 'ayin' he explains that help comes from above nature when no other help remains.

title.en: The Ruzhiner and the turning wheel

summary.en: The Mashgiach tells a story from the sefarim of Ruzhin: a chassid in deep trouble came weeping to the Ruzhiner, who told him of a merchant who wept when his lost money was found and danced when he had nothing left, because a wheel at the top must go down and at the bottom must rise. He ties it to 'me'ayin yavo ezri' and brings the Chesed L'Avraham that the geulah comes when Klal Yisrael can fall no lower.

title.en: The holy mountains and Yaakov's journey

summary.en: The Mashgiach brings explanations that the mountains are the holy mountains of Yerushalayim, and that without Yerushalayim a Jew can still be helped by turning to the Maker of heaven and earth. He brings the Midrash that Yaakov Avinu said this Shir Hamaalos when Eliphaz took all his money, reading 'harim' as the Avos, and explains that the Avos' levels were taken from them so that they would hold on to Hashem from a low state and teach this to their children.

catalogTitle: שיר למעלות אשא עיני

oneLiner.en: Learning Tehillim 121 and 122 as steps out of galus, the Mashgiach teaches that Hashem, the Shomer Yisrael who never sleeps, watches every Jew with hashgacha pratis, and that hopes for the geulah held on to in the dark will one day be remembered with joy.

abstract.en: The Mashgiach explains 'esa einai el heharim' as the cry of Jews who can no longer go up to the mountains of Zion: their help now comes directly from Hashem, Maker of 'heaven and earth', a name for the Beis Hamikdash, where the rules of number and nature did not apply. He brings the Midrash on Yaakov fleeing Esav with nothing, and reads 'He does not slumber' as Hashem staying awake through the sleep of galus. On 'Hashem is your shadow' he brings the Ba'al Shem Tov's teaching of hashgacha pratis: Hashem acts toward a Jew as the Jew acts, and one who trusts this does not lose by davening and learning properly. He places these psalms at the darkest end of galus, likens it to Adar, and promises protection in success and light in darkness. On Tehillim 122 he brings Makkos 10a, a story from Yerushalayim about children who 'talked kugel', and the Midrash that the Jews in Egypt comforted themselves on Shabbos with the promise of redemption.

en: With the mountains of Zion destroyed, a Jew's help comes directly from Hashem, who made 'heaven and earth', the Beis Hamikdash that stood above the rules of number and nature.
Galus is like sleep, but the Shomer Yisrael never sleeps and guards the one sheep among seventy wolves.
'Hashem is your shadow': Hashem deals with a Jew the way the Jew conducts himself, so one who lives by hashgacha pratis is shown hashgacha pratis.
The Ba'al Shem Tov did not invent belief in hashgacha pratis but made it shine in his students' hearts, down to which way a falling straw points.
The end of galus is its darkest part, like the blackness before dawn and like Adar at the end of the year, yet it is just there that things turn over.
Whatever a Jew's circumstances, success or its opposite, Hashem arranges them for his good, and if he believes it is good Hashem will show him that it is.
The hopes Jews spoke of in the hard days of galus, on Shabbos in Egypt and in poverty in Yerushalayim, will be recalled with joy when they come true.

candidateTopics: the darkest hour before the geulah

title.en: Help from the Maker of 'heaven and earth'

summary.en: The Mashgiach reads 'esa einai el heharim' as Jews who can no longer go up to the mountains of Zion, so their help comes straight from Hashem. He explains that the Beis Hamikdash is called 'heaven and earth' because, like heaven, it stood above the rules of number and nature, as seen in the miracle of room for everyone in Yerushalayim.

title.en: Yaakov's cry and the sleep of galus

summary.en: The Mashgiach brings the Midrash that Yaakov, robbed of everything while fleeing Esav, said 'esa einai el heharim', reading 'harim' as his parents. He then explains 'He will not slumber': galus is like sleep, but Hashem's heart is awake and He guards the one sheep among seventy wolves.

title.en: 'Hashem is your shadow'

summary.en: The Mashgiach brings the Midrash, often repeated by the Ba'al Shem Tov, that Hashem is a person's shadow and does what he does. A Jew who lives with hashgacha pratis does not cut short davening or learning for business, since he will not lose by serving Hashem, and he is shown hashgacha pratis openly.

title.en: Light that a teacher puts into a pasuk

summary.en: The Mashgiach asks why the Ba'al haTanya brings a known Midrash in the Ba'al Shem Tov's name, and answers that he received its light from him. He illustrates with the Gemara's peddler and 'mi ha'ish hechafetz chaim', the sign of 'pakod pakadti', the Ba'al Shem Tov's teaching on the falling straw, and a pasuk in Mishlei cited in a Tanna's name.

title.en: The darkest end of galus

summary.en: The Mashgiach places the Shir Hamaalos at the end of galus, its darkest part, like the blackness before dawn and like Adar at the end of the year, when Hashem is hidden yet things turn over. He reads 'by day the sun will not strike you, nor the moon by night' for the nation through its bright and dark periods, and explains that every Jew can find himself in every pasuk of Tehillim.

title.en: Guarded in success and in darkness

summary.en: The Mashgiach applies the end of the kapitel to the individual: one who fixes emunah in hashgacha pratis in himself is promised that his success will not harm him and that in his darkness Hashem will give him a moon. Hashem guards his going and coming forever, and arranges his circumstances for his good.

title.en: 'Samachti': remembering galus from the steps

summary.en: Starting Tehillim 122, the Mashgiach brings the Gemara that people asked when David would die so the Beis Hamikdash could be built, and David rejoiced at it. He then reads the kapitel as the redeemed climbing the steps recalling how they comforted each other in galus, illustrated by a story he heard about poor children in Yerushalayim who asked their mother to 'talk kugel'.

title.en: Shabbos comfort in Egypt

summary.en: The Mashgiach brings the Midrash on 'v'al yishu b'divrei sheker': Moshe won the Jews a day of rest, and on Shabbos they gathered and comforted each other with scrolls of the promises of redemption, which Pharaoh called 'words of falsehood' when he demanded the same output without straw. He concludes that those hopes have come true and 'our feet are standing in your gates, Yerushalayim'.

catalogTitle: Kashrus: An address to Organizations of Kashrus Overseers

oneLiner.en: The Mashgiach tells kashrus supervisors that, just as evil entered the world through food and Pharaoh made his food officials ministers of tumah, they are Heaven's appointed ministers of kedushah, who must work together without rivalry.

abstract.en: After a short introduction by the host, the Mashgiach recalls that Adam was meant to remain in Gan Eden, but was driven out for a sin of eating. Forbidden food, he explains, defiles the body and stops up the heart, becomes part of a person's very flesh and blood, and leaves no desire for Torah and tefillah; the Rema warns about this even for an infant. He then notes that Pharaoh, unlike a modern head of state, made the officials in charge of drink, bread and meat into ministers, because he knew that tumah is best spread through food. Yosef HaTzaddik was his counterpart in kedushah. Turning to the kashrus supervisors, the Mashgiach calls them the ministers of kedushah, cites the example of Rav Shraga Feivel Mendlowitz who supported other yeshivos, and warns against competition. He closes with the angels who visited Avraham Avinu, strengthened by his holy food for their mission to save Lot and the line of Moshiach.

en: Adam was driven from Gan Eden not for idolatry, immorality or bloodshed but for eating what he was forbidden to eat.
Forbidden food defiles the body, stops up the heart and becomes part of a person's flesh and blood, taking away his desire for Torah and tefillah.
Pharaoh made the officials over food into ministers of state because he knew that tumah spreads best through food.
The kashrus supervisors are Heaven's appointed ministers of kedushah and taharah, the counterpart of Pharaoh's ministers of food.
Ministers of one government must cooperate rather than compete, for they all serve the same Master.
A supervisor who is especially careful puts kedushah into all the food his company produces.

candidateTopics: the spiritual effect of forbidden food
Lot and the line of Moshiach

title.en: Adam's sin was a sin of eating

summary.en: After the host's introduction, the Mashgiach explains that Adam lost Gan Eden through eating forbidden food, and describes how forbidden food defiles the body, stops up the heart and removes the desire for Torah and tefillah.

title.en: Pharaoh's ministers of food

summary.en: The Mashgiach asks why Pharaoh had ministers over drink, bread and meat when a modern president only has a chef, and explains that Pharaoh, the master of tumah, knew that tumah is spread through food; Yosef HaTzaddik was his counterpart in kedushah.

title.en: Ministers of kedushah must not compete

summary.en: The Mashgiach tells the kashrus supervisors that they are the ministers of kedushah, brings the example of Rav Shraga Feivel Mendlowitz who sent his best talmidim to found other yeshivos, and warns that ministers who compete ruin their country; one cannot touch what is destined for another.

title.en: The angels strengthened by Avraham's food

summary.en: From the week's sedra the Mashgiach explains that angels too receive nourishment, and that the angels who ate at Avraham Avinu were fortified by the kedushah of his food for their dangerous mission to save Lot, from whom Moshiach descends. He closes by urging the supervisors to cooperate and sanctify the Jewish kitchen.

catalogTitle: שיר המעלות ... שמחתי באמרים לי

oneLiner.en: Going through Tehillim 122, the Mashgiach explains that Yerushalayim is built to match the Yerushalayim above, joins fear of Heaven with peace between people, stands above place, time and calculation, and is the name of every Jew, so a Jew must care about Jews everywhere.

abstract.en: The Mashgiach reads Tehillim 122 verse by verse. 'Our feet stood in your gates' describes a person transfixed by the sight of the rebuilt city, and also the merit of those learning in Yerushalayim, which wins Israel's wars. 'Built like a city joined together' means Yerushalayim below is built to match Yerushalayim above, which is why, he says, the Old City's twisting streets were rebuilt exactly as before; nothing in holiness is random, just as Teveria's name and the shape of the human body each have a reason. The city's two names, from Shem and Avraham, join peace and fear of Heaven, matching the Chasam Sofer's point that Yerushalayim joins duties to Hashem and to people. The tribes rise there above their divisions to the level of Yaakov, and above place, time and calculation. The Davidic kings may sit in the Azarah because of their humility. Finally, 'ask for the peace of Yerushalayim' teaches that every Jew must care about Jews everywhere.

en: The Mashgiach explains 'Yerushalayim habenuyah' to mean that Yerushalayim below is built exactly to match Yerushalayim and the Beis HaMikdash above.
He teaches that every matter of holiness is exactly as it is in Heaven and has a reason, from the streets of the Old City to the name Teveria and the structure of the human body.
Yerushalayim joins the two names Shem and Avraham gave it, peace and fear of Heaven, and so it joins duties between man and Hashem with duties between man and his fellow.
Yerushalayim was not divided among the tribes; it is the place of Yaakov, the trunk from which the tribes branch out, and in coming there the tribes were raised above their own level.
The Davidic kings could judge and sit in the Azarah because they were humble and nullified, so that they themselves are Yerushalayim.
Since all Jews are called Yerushalayim, 'ask for the peace of Yerushalayim' means a Jew must take interest in what happens to Jews everywhere.

the name Yerushalayim: Yir'eh and Shalem
kings of the House of David
bitul as the foundation of avodah

title.en: Joy fulfilled and feet that stand still

summary.en: The Mashgiach opens with 'samachti b'omrim li': the longing heard in exile is fulfilled when one stands in Yerushalayim. He brings Rav Shimshon Raphael Hirsch that a person seeing the rebuilt city stops in his tracks, and the meforshim that the soldiers win by the merit of those learning in Yerushalayim's gates, which he applies to those who demand drafting yeshiva students.

title.en: A city joined to the Yerushalayim above

summary.en: The Mashgiach gives two readings of 'k'ir shechubrah lah yachdav': holiness breaks through its walls so that its surroundings join it, and Yerushalayim below is built to match Yerushalayim above, where Michael serves as kohen gadol. He connects this to the halachos of building the Mishkan and Mikdash and to the Rambam that all Yerushalayim has a din of Mikdash.

title.en: Why the Old City was rebuilt as it was

summary.en: The Mashgiach describes the Old City after the Six-Day War, with its narrow twisting alleys, and how the man in charge of rebuilding it, a German Jew with a sense for history, rebuilt it street by street as before to preserve its antiquity. The Mashgiach explains that Hashem put this idea into his head because Yerushalayim must match the Yerushalayim above, and everyone does Hashem's errand.

title.en: Nothing in holiness is by chance

summary.en: The Mashgiach brings the Gemara's reason for the name Teveria, 'tovah re'iyasah', though Chazal knew the wicked Tiberius named it after himself, and the Rambam that the Sanhedrin will first return to Teveria. He then explains that the human body, the tzelem Elokim of 248 limbs, has a reason for every twist, as the face forms Hashem's Name, and so too the streets of Yerushalayim.

title.en: Fear of Heaven joined with peace

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that Yerushalayim joins the names given by two tzaddikim, Shalem by Shem and Yir'eh by Avraham. He brings the Chasam Sofer that some lands stress service of G-d and others only decency between people, while Yerushalayim holds both, as the next verses show: the tribes go up to thank Hashem, and the thrones of judgment are there.

title.en: The tribes rise to the place of Yaakov

summary.en: The Mashgiach brings the Gemara that Yerushalayim was not divided among the tribes. Yaakov, linked with Shabbos, is the trunk and the tribes are the branches; Eretz Yisroel is the place of the tribes and Yerushalayim the place of Yaakov, so on the Yomim Tovim the tribes went up and were raised above the level of a tribe.

title.en: Above place, time and calculation

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that Yerushalayim is like an extension of Heaven, where the laws of mathematics do not apply: no one ever said the place was too crowded, those standing pressed together bowed with room to spare, and the Aron took up no space. The 'shivtei Kah' carry the Name Kah, which is above place, time and calculation.

title.en: The thrones of the House of David

summary.en: The Mashgiach brings the Mishnah that a king neither judges nor is judged, from the episode of Yannai and Shimon ben Shetach, while the Davidic kings could judge because they humbly stood to be judged; likewise only they may sit in the Azarah, because they are nullified to it. He explains bitul as a foundation of avodah, and resolves the Brisker Rav's question on the closing of the brachah for Yerushalayim: David is Yerushalayim.

title.en: Ask after the peace of every Jew

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains 'sha'alu shalom Yerushalayim': the holiness of the Mikdash spreads over all Yerushalayim, and the Midrash calls all Jews Yerushalayim, so a Jew must take interest in Jews in Russia, Africa, Iraq and Teiman as one worries over a brother who stopped writing. He ends with 'for the sake of my brothers and friends' and 'for the sake of the House of Hashem', a prayer for both the place and the souls.

catalogTitle: שיר המעלות אליך נשאתי

oneLiner.en: Going through Tehillim 123, 'Shir hamaalos elecha nasasi es einai', the Mashgiach explains what it means that Hashem Himself is a Jew's mivtach, how a servant looks only to the hand that strikes him, and why Klal Yisrael cries out a double 'chaneinu' from the shame of galus.

abstract.en: The Mashgiach reads 'elecha nasasi es einai hayoshvi bashamayim' as David HaMelech speaking for Klal Yisrael in galus. He brings the Ba'al Shem Tov on 'vehayah Hashem mivtacho': a person must do his hishtadlus, but Hashem, not the business, must be the mivtach. Two stories illustrate it, the Ba'al Shem Tov knocking at a wealthy man's door and Reb Pinchas of Koretz throwing back a coin, and they explain Rashi on Yosef's two extra years in prison. 'Hayoshvi' means my own G-d in heaven, and bitachon must never stop. Like servants looking to their master's hand, a Jew who suffers turns to the One who sends the suffering. Through the hanging ayin of 'chazir miya'ar' he shows how galus can be turned around. The double 'chaneinu' is a reflexive cry, like 'maher maher' and Eliyahu's 'aneini aneini'. Finally, with Rav Shimshon Raphael Hirsch, he explains galus as a mission to the nations, borne with pride despite their scorn.

en: Following the Ba'al Shem Tov, a person must do hishtadlus, but Hashem Himself must be his mivtach, the one his hope rests on, not his business.
Yosef was kept two more years in prison for relying on the sar hamashkim because more is demanded of a tzaddik of his level.
'Hayoshvi bashamayim' expresses each Jew's personal G-d in heaven who watches over him with individual hashgachah, which gives him security.
Like a servant whose only hope is the master who strikes him, a Jew who suffers turns to Hashem who sends the suffering and asks Him for grace.
Repeated words in tefillah, 'maher maher' and the double 'chaneinu', are an inner cry, a reflex of a person who can no longer bear the pain, not an addition to the text.
Jews went into galus in the service of Hashem, to bring emunah and good middos to the nations, and they keep their pride and bitachon despite the nations' scorn.

galus as a mission to the nations

title.en: Hayoshvi bashamayim and the Ba'al Shem Tov on mivtach

summary.en: The Mashgiach opens the kapitel as David HaMelech speaking for the Jews in galus and notes the poetic extra yud in 'hayoshvi'. He then brings the Ba'al Shem Tov on 'vehayah Hashem mivtacho': one who hopes, the one he relies on, and the thing he hopes for; a person must do something for parnassah, but Hashem, not the business, must be the mivtach.

title.en: The Ba'al Shem Tov, Reb Pinchas of Koretz and Yosef

summary.en: The Mashgiach tells how the young Ba'al Shem Tov knocked once at a wealthy man's door and left, having done his hishtadlus, and how Reb Pinchas of Koretz threw back a coin he found and then received it from a wealthy man. With the Biala Rebbe's comment and Rashi on Yosef's two extra years in prison, he explains that more is demanded of a tzaddik like Yosef.

title.en: My own G-d in heaven; bitachon without pause

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that 'hayoshvi' is not only ornament: Klal Yisrael says 'my One who sits in heaven', a personal G-d with individual hashgachah, and so feels secure. From the pause after 'einai' and the ta'amim he learns that a Jew's bitachon must continue without stop, even after he has done his part and even when by reason there is no hope.

title.en: Eyes of servants to the master's hand

summary.en: On 'hinei ke'einei avadim', the Mashgiach explains that 'ad sheyechaneinu' asks for free grace, and brings the Radak: a servant struck by his master can hope only that the striking hand itself will stop and pardon him. So a Jew who suffers turns to Hashem who sends it; with 'im kevanim im ka'avadim' and the Kedushas Levi, Klal Yisrael asks to be treated again as children.

title.en: The hanging ayin of chazir miya'ar

summary.en: By way of drush the Mashgiach brings 'yechar'semenah chazir miya'ar' with its raised ayin, and Rashi that the forest boar is Rome, which destroys when punishment is decreed on Israel. If Israel merits, the ayin becomes an aleph and the forest boar a helpless river creature; he connects this to the 'kosnos or' with an aleph in Rabbi Meir's Torah, and to the plea 'chaneinu Hashem chaneinu'.

title.en: The scorn of galus and the double 'maher'

summary.en: On 'ki rav savanu vuz' the Mashgiach describes the nations' contempt, the doctrine that the Jews are cursed wanderers who will never have Yerushalayim, which he says is behind the uproar over Yerushalayim. He then asks how one may say 'maher maher' twice when the Anshei Knesses HaGedolah, among them prophets, measured every word, and brings an example of an 'oy' cried out in the middle of davening.

title.en: A reflexive cry: 'quick, quick' and 'aneini aneini'

summary.en: The Mashgiach gives a parable of a child outside who sees a tiger and cries 'Father, quick!' and then 'quick!' again: the second cry adds nothing, it is a reflex like 'ouch'. So the second 'maher' and the second 'chaneinu' are an inner cry, and he shows the same from the Gemara in Taanis on Eliyahu's 'aneini aneini', where the second word is the cry.

title.en: Turning the cheek; sated with scorn

summary.en: The Mashgiach brings a later author on 'yiten lemakeihu lechi yisba becherpah': when the one struck offers his cheek, the striker is satisfied with the disgrace and stops striking. So Klal Yisrael says it is already sated with the shame of galus, 'rabbas sav'ah lah nafsheinu', the mockery of the complacent nations and the scorn toward the defenseless dove.

title.en: Galus as a mission; proud beggars

summary.en: Following Rav Shimshon Raphael Hirsch, the Mashgiach explains that Jews are in galus in Hashem's service, to be a light to the nations; in Shlomo's time the nations came to them, and now, not having merited, Jews must go to the nations, as he brings from the Chasam Sofer and the Gemara. In that service they bear scorn but keep their pride and bitachon, mocked as 'proud beggars', until Hashem brings them back to Tziyon.

catalogTitle: Emunah - The Everlasting Essence of a Jewish Heart

oneLiner.en: The Mashgiach opens a series on the mitzvah of emunah, explaining that it is the foundation of all the mitzvos and a hereditary trait inherited from Avraham Avinu, a spark that cannot be extinguished in any Jewish heart.

abstract.en: The Mashgiach describes how, decades ago, he began teaching the mitzvos from the Sefer Chareidim, which arranges them by the limbs of the body and opens the mitzvos of the heart with emunah; over time his notes grew until he taught only emunah for a whole year. Emunah, he says, must be spoken about and fed constantly, like daily food, citing Yirmiyahu and Tehillim, and former students later thanked him for preparing them for challenges. Emunah is the first of the Ten Commandments and is renewed through Shema. He presents the dispute of the Rambam, who counts emunah among the 613 mitzvos, and the Ramban, who sees it as their prerequisite, since it is not phrased as a command. To approach the Rambam he distinguishes acquired from hereditary knowledge, using the bee, beaver and spider, and says emunah is a Jew's hereditary instinct from Sinai and Avraham Avinu. A kashya on this, like a helium balloon to a child, does not disprove it.

en: Emunah is the first mitzvah of the heart in the Sefer Chareidim and the first of the Ten Commandments, which shows it is the most important mitzvah.
Emunah must be constantly fortified and fed, just as a person cannot eat one breakfast for his whole life.
The Rambam counts emunah among the 613 mitzvos, while the Ramban holds it is above them, their foundation and prerequisite, since without emunah no act is a mitzvah.
Some knowledge is hereditary rather than acquired, as with the bee, the beaver and the spider, and emunah in a Jew is such a hereditary instinct.
Every Jew's soul remembers hearing 'Anochi Hashem' at Sinai, and Jews inherited emunah from Avraham Avinu, so a spark of emunah remains in every Jewish heart.

title.en: The Sefer Chareidim's order of the mitzvos

summary.en: The Mashgiach recalls beginning to teach the mitzvos from the Sefer Chareidim, which arranges them by the limbs of the body rather than by the order of the Torah. He explains that the heart governs the emotional mitzvos such as tefillah, dveikus and love of Hashem, and that the first mitzvah of the heart is emunah.

title.en: Emunah must be fed constantly

summary.en: The Mashgiach tells how his shiurim narrowed until he taught only the mitzvah of emunah for a whole year. Citing Yirmiyahu's rebuke and the passuk in Tehillim, he says emunah must be spoken about and nourished daily, and recounts how former students thanked him years later for preparing them for challenges to their emunah.

title.en: Rambam and Ramban: is emunah one of the 613?

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that emunah is the first of the Ten Commandments and is renewed through Shema several times a day. He presents the dispute of the Rambam, who counts emunah as a mitzvah, and the Ramban, who calls it the prerequisite of all the mitzvos, illustrated by tzedakah given without emunah. He adds that every mitzvah is phrased as a command while 'Anochi' is a statement, which seems to support the Ramban, and says the Rambam's view must be understood.

title.en: Hereditary knowledge: the bee, the beaver, the spider

summary.en: The Mashgiach distinguishes hereditary traits such as hair color from acquired knowledge such as a sugya in Bava Metzia, then shows that some knowledge is inherited: a bee builds a honeycomb, a beaver a dam and a spider a web without being taught. He concludes that emunah in a Jew is such a hereditary instinct.

title.en: A spark of emunah from Sinai and Avraham Avinu

summary.en: The Mashgiach says every Jew's soul remembers hearing 'Anochi Hashem' at Sinai, and that Avraham Avinu, the first believer, completed creation, so Jews are believers the sons of believers. He raises the kashya of Jews who do not believe and, with the mashal of a child seeing a helium balloon rise, explains that a kashya does not disprove an absolute truth. He closes that a spark of emunah in every Jewish heart cannot be extinguished, deferring the answers to the next shiur.

catalogTitle: שיר המעלות ... לולי ה' שהיה לנו

oneLiner.en: Through Tehillim 124 and 125, the Mashgiach explains that the Jewish people survive their exile because they recognize Hashem's hand in everything and trust in Him, and that their holiness, like Yerushalayim's, comes from the Shechinah and can never be taken away.

abstract.en: The Mashgiach opens with a remez on why the first blessing of Shemoneh Esrei says 'Elokei Yaakov' and not Yisrael, then reads Tehillim 124. Only a Jew who sees Hashem's providence in everything can say 'Had Hashem not been with us'. He brings the Gemara that 'a man rose against us' means Haman, a man with free choice rather than a king, and explains the floods, Rashi on the splitting of all waters at the Yam Suf, and the trap that broke. The nations that fought the Jews were broken, while the Jews revived again and again; he describes the sinking of pre-war American Jewry like Pisom and Raamses, tells of a Jew who would not work on Shabbos, and the rebirth of Torah after the war. 'Our help is in Hashem's Name' means recognizing that He constantly renews creation. In Tehillim 125 he explains Har Tziyon and, with the Rambam, that Yerushalayim's and Klal Yisrael's holiness comes from the Shechinah and is never annulled.

en: Only a Jew for whom Hashem's Name is constantly on his lips, who sees Hashem's providence in everything, can say 'Had Hashem not been with us', unlike the nations who credit luck.
The Gemara reads 'a man rose against us' as Haman: a man has free choice and is harder to be saved from than a king, whose heart is in Hashem's hand.
The nations that attacked the Jews were all broken in the end, while the Jewish people survived and revived after every trouble, including after the Nazis.
Jews survive in exile through recognizing that Hashem is with them and runs the world; the more they know it, the more help they have.
Those who trust in Hashem are like Har Tziyon, which never moves; even in exile they are protected as the mountains surround Yerushalayim.

According to the Rambam, Yerushalayim's holiness comes from the Shechinah and was never annulled; Klal Yisrael's holiness likewise comes from the Shechinah dwelling among them and no conquest or sin can take it away.

title.en: Who can say 'Had Hashem not been with us'

summary.en: The Mashgiach opens with a remez from sefarim on why Shemoneh Esrei says 'Elokei Yaakov' rather than Yisrael, then reads the start of Tehillim 124. He asks who it is that says 'Had Hashem not been with us' and answers: a Jew who sees Hashem's providence in everything, unlike the nations who speak of luck.

title.en: Haman, the floods and the broken trap

summary.en: The Mashgiach brings the Gemara that 'a man rose against us' is Haman and explains why a man with free choice is more dangerous than a king. He explains the floods as forces of judgment that split before the Jews by the eternal power of the Yam Suf, and the bird escaping the broken trap, which the meforshim apply to the Beis HaMikdash; the nations that fought the Jews were all broken.

title.en: Pre-war America like Pisom and Raamses

summary.en: The Mashgiach speaks of the unrecognized wonder of Torah's growth after the Nazi destruction, and contrasts pre-war America, which he likens to Pisom and Raamses built on sinking ground. He tells that of about forty boys in his yeshiva class only four remained Shabbos-observant, and describes the immigrants who had to work on Shabbos to keep a job.

title.en: Holding on to Shabbos in America

summary.en: The Mashgiach tells of a Williamsburg Jew who would not work on Shabbos, and of an old Jew who, ready to give in for his family's sake, saw bread in a garbage can and resolved not to work on Shabbos as long as there was bread there; in the end Hashem helped him. He adds that those who could got a pushcart license, while millions sank and their children did not stay Jewish.

title.en: The rebirth after the war

summary.en: The Mashgiach describes how the youth of his own shul sank, and how after the war refugees and great leaders like the Satmar Rav, the Klausenburger Rav, Rabbi Yonasan Steif and the Vizhnitzer Rebbe rebuilt Yiddishkeit here and in Eretz Yisrael. He calls it a techiyas hameisim of a people that is taken for granted, and explains that the trap broke and the Jews came out whole, not like a bird that escapes with a broken wing.

title.en: What sustains the Jews in exile

summary.en: The Mashgiach asks what keeps the Jews alive in exile and answers from the opening and close of the kapitel: recognizing that Hashem is with us and runs the world, 'our help is in the Name of Hashem, Maker of heaven and earth'. 'Maker' in the present means He constantly renews creation, so that, as the talmidei haBa'al Shem Tov say, a decree can be absent from the new heavens. He then begins Tehillim 125: those who trust in Hashem are like Har Tziyon, built on rock, which never moves.

title.en: Tziyon as a mark of G-dliness

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that the mountains around Yerushalayim are a natural protection, and so Hashem surrounds His people. He brings Rav Samson Raphael Hirsch that Tziyon means a marker: from there the knowledge of one G-d went out into the world, and those who trust in Hashem take over that role in exile, firm and unmoving.

title.en: Holiness that comes from the Shechinah

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains the Rambam's view that the holiness of Eretz Yisrael that came from Yehoshua's conquest was annulled when Nevuchadnetzar conquered it, but Yerushalayim's holiness comes from the Shechinah and remains. So too Klal Yisrael is holy because the Shechinah dwells among them, and no conquest by the nations can remove it. A Jew who knows this, that he is a part of G-d above, will not sin and drag the Shechinah into exile.

catalogTitle: שיר המעלות הבטחים בה'

oneLiner.en: Through the last verses of Shir HaMa'alos HaBotchim and the opening of Shir HaMa'alos B'shuv, the Mashgiach explains why tzaddikim accept Heaven's decrees, why each soul is held to the Torah at its own level, and why the redemption will be 'like a dream'.

abstract.en: The Mashgiach explains 'the rod of the wicked will not rest on the lot of the tzaddikim': the rule of the wicked is only temporary, so tzaddikim do not raise their hands against it. He shows this in the tzaddikim of the Spanish expulsion, the Ten Martyrs, the tzaddikim of the war years and a story of the Ruzhiner. On 'do good to the good and the upright in heart' he contrasts true good people with hypocrites, and tells how the Kotzker eased a scoffer out of Rebbe Reb Bunim's chevra. From the washing of hands in the morning he develops that souls and Torah have levels: the Shulchan Aruch is the minimum, and for a higher person lifnim mishuras hadin becomes the law, as in the story of Rabbah bar bar Chanah. Therefore one should not mock the chumros of greater Jews. Finally he gives several explanations of 'we were like dreamers'.

en: The rule of the wicked over the tzaddikim is only temporary, so tzaddikim do not stretch out their hands to fight it but accept the decree and rely on Hashem.
Great tzaddikim who had the power to overturn kingdoms asked in Heaven, were told it was a decree, and accepted it.
David HaMelech asks Hashem to do good to those who are upright through and through, and to lead the crooked hypocrites away so they do not mix with honest Jews.
Souls and the Torah both have levels; the Shulchan Aruch is the minimum, and each person must keep the Torah according to his level.
What is lifnim mishuras hadin (beyond the letter of the law) for an ordinary person is the law itself for a person of a higher level.
One should not mock or criticize chumros of greater Jews or of a Rebbe's followers, since they stem from a higher level or from bond to the Rebbe.
'We were like dreamers' means that the redemption will surpass every dream, and that its joy will make the whole galus seem like a dream.

title.en: The rod of the wicked is only temporary

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that the rule of the wicked over the tzaddikim is temporary, so tzaddikim do not raise their hands against it but rely on Hashem. He brings the tzaddikim of the Spanish expulsion, who could have overturned Spain but were told in Heaven it was a decree and accepted it.

title.en: The Ten Martyrs, the war years and the Ruzhiner

summary.en: The Mashgiach asks why the Ten Martyrs, who could have destroyed Rome, let themselves be killed, and answers that Heaven told them it was the decree. He adds the tzaddikim of the war who accepted the decree, and tells how the Ruzhiner, fleeing the Czar, did not use his power against Russia because Russia had once taken in fleeing Jews.

title.en: The truly good and the hypocrites

summary.en: On 'do good, Hashem, to the good and to the upright in their hearts' the Mashgiach explains that the good are those who are good through and through, unlike hypocrites who only put on a fine face. David HaMelech asks that the crooked be led away from the honest, and the Mashgiach begins the account of Rebbe Reb Bunim's chevra of great minds.

title.en: The Kotzker and the scoffer

summary.en: The Mashgiach tells how the Kotzker saw that a brilliant newcomer lacked emunas tzaddikim and mocked the Ba'er Heitev's words on walking without washing the hands, and gently persuaded him to leave the chevra. He returns to the verse, 'lead them away... peace upon Israel', and to the care Chassidim take with washing the hands at the bed.

title.en: Levels of souls and levels of Torah

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that pshat, remez, drush and sod correspond to nefesh, ruach, neshamah and chayah, so both a stringent sefer and a lenient posek are right, each for its level. The Shulchan Aruch is the minimum; Yerushalayim, being higher, was destroyed for keeping only the letter of the law. A stain that does not matter on a potato sack ruins silk, and a Gemara that seems exaggerated speaks of a higher person.

title.en: For a higher person, beyond the law is the law

summary.en: From the steps to the mizbe'ach counted as uncovering nakedness, the Mashgiach shows that for an oved Hashem pride is like giluy arayos. He tells the Gemara's story of Rabbah bar bar Chanah and the porters, where Rav told him that for him lifnim mishuras hadin is the law, and reads 'v'eileh hamishpatim asher tasim lifneihem' the same way. He applies it to waiting between meat and milk.

title.en: The Belzer Rav's grapes; do not mock chumros

summary.en: The Mashgiach tells of the Belzer Rav, who would not eat grapes a host in Boro Park had obtained for him in winter, because the plate had not been toiveled. He concludes that one must not mock or criticize the chumros of greater Jews, and brings the Gemara in Sukkah that Rav Kahana's students followed even his leniency on hadassim as a bond to their Rebbe.

title.en: 'We were like dreamers'

summary.en: The Mashgiach opens Shir HaMa'alos B'shuv and gives several explanations of 'we were like dreamers': the redemption will exceed all we imagined, as real food exceeds a prisoner's dream; it will be like the impossible sights of a dream; its joy will make galus seem a dream; and, in a pshat he attributes to Rav Shimshon Raphael Hirsch, we will then discover the tikunim Jews achieved for the world in galus.

catalogTitle: שיר המעלות בשוב ה' את שיבת ציון

oneLiner.en: The Mashgiach explains Shir HaMa'alos, 'B'shuv Hashem es shivas Tziyon', as the joy of a geulah that will make the long galus seem like a dream and reveal that the Jews' greatness, influence and tears in exile were all planting for the redemption, and then turns to 'Shir HaMa'alos l'Shlomo' and why the Beis HaMikdash built by man had to be destroyed.

abstract.en: The Mashgiach reads 'B'shuv Hashem es shivas Tziyon hayinu k'cholmim': the geulah will exceed all dreams, and the bitter galus will pass like a dream one wakes from. In galus Jews feel mocked and powerless, yet their influence, which he explains through Rav Yaakov Kamenetsky's reading of the word hashpa'ah, flows down on the nations and on less observant Jews, as the Rambam shows; this is the 'light to the nations'. Citing Rebbe Nachman, he says the greatness is with the Jews even now, and when Moshiach comes the Jews will laugh at the nations' limited understanding. He describes the longing in 'Shuvah Hashem es shevisenu', the Ba'al HaTanya's teaching that thirst in galus exceeds that of Temple times, and the tears that are seeds of the geulah, with Rebbe Zusha's vort on sowing in tears or in joy. He then turns to 'Shir HaMa'alos l'Shlomo': the Beis HaMikdash built by human hands had to fall, all within Hashem's plan, so that the Kosel Maaravi and its kedushah would remain.

en: The geulah will surpass every dream, and the long galus will then seem like a passing dream.
Even when Jews feel powerless and mocked in galus, their influence flows down on the nations and on less observant Jews, and this is why Hashem sent them into galus, to be a light to the nations.
The true greatness is with the Jews even in galus; when Moshiach comes this will be revealed, and the nations' limited grasp of it will be cause for laughter.
The longing of Jews in galus is greater than in Temple times, and that longing, with their Torah, tefillos and tears, is itself the seed that brings the geulah.
The Beis HaMikdash built by human hands could not last; its destruction was part of Hashem's plan, and the true Beis HaMikdash Hashem Himself will build.

According to the Yismach Moshe, the Beis HaMikdash was built so that, after its destruction, the Kosel Maaravi would remain, where the Shechinah stays and on which the Jews' existence in galus depends.

title.en: The geulah will be like a dream

summary.en: The Mashgiach begins 'B'shuv Hashem es shivas Tziyon hayinu k'cholmim' and explains that the geulah will exceed all dreams, while the bitter galus will pass like a dream one wakes from. The great prophecies of the nevi'im, he says, are nothing compared to what will actually be.

title.en: The hidden influence of Jews in galus

summary.en: The Mashgiach describes how in galus Jews feel they accomplish nothing, surrounded by enemies and scoffers who mock even ehrliche Yidden. He explains, through Rav Yaakov Kamenetsky's reading of the word hashpa'ah, that their influence flows down on the nations and on less observant Jews, and that this is the purpose of galus, to be a light to the nations, as seen in the Rambam.

title.en: Then our mouths will fill with laughter

summary.en: On 'Az yimalei s'chok pinu' the Mashgiach says the Jews will laugh last, and their speech will turn to song. Bringing Rebbe Nachman of Breslov and a mashal of a prince disciplined by servants, he explains that the greatness is with the Jews even in galus, and that when Moshiach comes the nations will grasp it only in a limited way, which is why the Jews will laugh at them.

title.en: Longing for the geulah like streams in the Negev

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains 'Shuvah Hashem es shevisenu' as a tefilah said with thirst and longing for the days of Moshiach, a longing he says has weakened even among bnei Torah, and brings the Midrash that the Jews in Mitzrayim spoke on Shabbos of the coming redemption. He explains 'ka'afikim banegev' and brings the Ba'al HaTanya that the thirst of Jews in galus for Hashem is greater than in the time of the Beis HaMikdash, like a person in a desert compared with one who knows water is at hand.

title.en: Sowing in tears, reaping in joy

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that the Torah, avodah, tefillos, longing and tears of Jews in galus are seeds of the geulah, and that even in galus Jews rejoiced, like a sheep among seventy wolves. He brings Rebbe Zusha's vort on serving Hashem with tears or with joy, and the Midrash that Israel in galus is called Yizre'el, planting belief in Hashem among the nations, for which they will be rewarded when galus ends.

title.en: Shir HaMa'alos l'Shlomo and the first Beis HaMikdash

summary.en: The Mashgiach turns to 'Shir HaMa'alos l'Shlomo', which Dovid HaMelech composed about the Beis HaMikdash his son would build and which would not last, and retells from Chazal how Shlomo's marriage to Pharaoh's daughter delayed the morning tamid and how Gavriel planted the reed from which Rome grew. He insists Shlomo is not understood and acted l'shem shamayim, and explains 'Im Hashem lo yivneh bayis': only what Hashem builds endures.

title.en: A Mikdash built by man had to fall

summary.en: Bringing Rashi on 'Mikdash Hashem konenu yadecha' and something he heard from a tzaddik, the Mashgiach explains that the Beis HaMikdash was destroyed because a human hand built it; Shlomo only appears to be the cause. Like the sale of Yosef, the sin of the Eitz HaDa'as and the meraglim, it was all in Hashem's plan, which will be understood when Moshiach comes. He adds Rashi's explanation that the third Beis HaMikdash will come down from heaven.

title.en: Built to leave the Kosel Maaravi

summary.en: The Mashgiach brings the Yismach Moshe that the Beis HaMikdash was built to be destroyed so that the Kosel Maaravi would remain, where the Shechinah never departs, and the Arvei Nachal that all the kedushah of the Mikdash lies hidden under the Kosel. He closes with the Rambam that the kedushah of Yerushalayim and the Mikdash is never nullified, since it comes from the Shechinah.

catalogTitle: Emunah - Concealed Behind Layers of Rationalization and Impurity

oneLiner.en: The Mashgiach explains that every Jew inherits emunah from Avraham Avinu, and that a Jew who denies Hashem is only covering his inner belief with a layer of rationalization, which is what the word 'kofer' means.

abstract.en: The Mashgiach begins with the point of the previous week: a Jew has emunah by inheritance, the way a newborn instinctively knows how to nurse and a migrating bird finds its way back to the same tree, and the ba'al teshuvah's return to his roots shows it. He then asks why so many Jews declare that they do not believe. His answer is that they do believe, but disbelief is comfortable, so they suppress their emunah through rationalization. He explains rationalization with the fable of the wolf and the sour grapes, everyday examples, and the story of Chiel of Beis El, who explained away the death of his sons. He contrasts people driven by taivah, who do teshuvah in old age, with those driven by ga'avah, who never admit their mistake. He then explains Avraham Avinu as a new species that believes in Hashem, which is why the Avos were barren and why a hey was added to Avraham's name. Finally he explains that a kofer is one who covers over the truth, like the tar on Noach's ark.

en: Every Jew has emunah by inheritance from the Avos, like the knowledge animals and infants are born with rather than learn.
A Jew who declares that he does not believe is not telling the truth: he believes, but finds it comfortable not to, and suppresses his emunah.
Rationalization means that a person's ego will not let him admit his own fault, so he blames something else.
Whether a person does teshuvah in old age depends on whether his dominant drive is taivah or ga'avah.
Avraham Avinu was a new species, a human being who naturally believes in Hashem, and the hey added to his name gave him the power to continue that species.
A kofer is one who covers over a truth he knows inside; his heresy is only a veneer.

title.en: Emunah as an inherited instinct

summary.en: The Mashgiach recalls that the children of Avraham, Yitzchak and Yaakov have emunah by inheritance, and compares it to a newborn who knows how to nurse and a bird that finds its way back to the same tree. He sees the same instinct in ba'alei teshuvah returning to their roots.

title.en: Why do Jews deny? Rationalization

summary.en: The Mashgiach asks why so many Jews say they do not believe, and answers that they do believe but suppress it, through the psychological law of rationalization. He notes that all of psychology is in the Torah, with the Chazon Ish's answer about psychology books, and explains rationalization with the fable of the wolf and the sour grapes.

title.en: Examples of rationalization: Chiel of Beis El

summary.en: The Mashgiach gives everyday examples of blaming something else, a bochur who blames the lighting and an inexperienced sukkah builder who blames the hammer, and then tells how Chiel of Beis El rebuilt Yericho despite Yehoshua's curse and found an excuse for the death of each son.

title.en: Taivah, ga'avah and teshuvah in old age

summary.en: After the bird that hides its head in the sand, the Mashgiach describes old people in a nursing home who return to Yiddishkeit once they can no longer indulge, and explains that those driven by taivah do teshuvah while those driven by ga'avah never admit their life was folly. A weak person who does not want to fight his yetzer says the fault is in religion.

title.en: Avraham Avinu, a new species of believer

summary.en: The Mashgiach says that a professed atheist really believes, because every Jew inherits the emunah of Avraham Avinu, of whom the Torah first says that he believed in Hashem. He explains that Avraham was a new species, severed from the previous generations, which is why he was barren and needed the hey added to his name, as with Sarah and Bilhah.

title.en: A kofer covers over the truth

summary.en: The Mashgiach sums up that the believing Jew is a new kind of being, which is why the Avos had to be barren. He then explains that 'kofer' means one who covers over a truth he knows, like the kofer (tar) smeared on Noach's ark and the kapores covering the aron, and concludes that every Jew believes deep down, as believers the children of believers.

catalogTitle: שיר המעלות לשלמה

oneLiner.en: The Mashgiach explains Shir HaMa'alos l'Shlomo and the next chapter, Ashrei kol yerei Hashem: everything depends on Hashem's help, children are a blessing and a source of parnassah, and the happiness of a Jew lies in a home run by the Torah.

abstract.en: The Mashgiach opens with the psalm David HaMelech composed for Shlomo about the Beis HaMikdash: because Shlomo slept late on the night before its inauguration, the churban was already set in motion, and 'if Hashem does not build the house' speaks of that destruction. A house, a city and a livelihood all need siyata dishmaya. He applies 'it is vain for you who rise early' to people who give all their strength to business and leave no time for davening and learning, bringing the Midrash about the mann. He then explains that some events are part of Hashem's plan from before creation, so Shlomo is not to be blamed, and David calls him a gift from Hashem. In a second reading the chapter is about bitachon: children bring parnassah, youth is precious like arrows in a warrior's hand, and even the mud children bring in is a blessing. Finally, he explains chapter 128: the happiness of an honest, content Jewish home, a modest wife and children around the table.

en: The Mashgiach explains that 'if Hashem does not build the house' speaks of the destruction of the Beis HaMikdash, which began with Shlomo sleeping late on the night before its inauguration.
A person, a household, a city and a business all need siyata dishmaya; without it effort is in vain.
Those who rise early and stay up late for business, leaving no time for proper davening and learning, labor in vain, because what is decreed for a person he will receive.
Some events, like the churban, Moshe not entering Eretz Yisrael and the sale of Yosef, were set in Hashem's plan before creation, so they are not a punishment and Shlomo is not to be blamed.
For a G-d-fearing Jew children are a blessing: each child brings a new channel of parnassah.
The years of youth are precious, like arrows in a warrior's hand: once they have passed they cannot be recaptured.
Chapter 128 shows the happiness of a Jew who lives by the Torah: honest earnings, a modest wife, children around the table, and contentment in this world and the next.

title.en: A psalm for Shlomo about the Beis HaMikdash

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that David composed this psalm for Shlomo about the Beis HaMikdash, which was destroyed because it began badly: Shlomo slept late on the night before its inauguration. 'If Hashem does not build the house' speaks of the churban, and he concludes that a person, a home and a city all need siyata dishmaya.

title.en: Rising early for business in vain

summary.en: The Mashgiach applies 'it is vain for you who rise early' to people who pour all their strength into business and leave no time for davening, learning and their children's chinuch. He brings the Midrash about the mann and a tzaddik's question to a man running to his livelihood, and says business needs no hiddurim; a Jew with bitachon lives an orderly life and eats his bread with simcha.

title.en: Hashem's plan, and Shlomo is not to blame

summary.en: The Mashgiach asks how David could speak this way about his son Shlomo, and answers that some things are part of Hashem's plan from before creation and are not a punishment, citing the Ohr HaChaim and the Midrash Tanchuma: Moshe and the rock, Adam and the Eitz HaDa'as, the sale of Yosef and the two churbanos. Only by the greatest tzaddikim does this happen, and so David continues 'behold, children are the heritage of Hashem', proud of his son Shlomo.

title.en: Bitachon: children bring parnassah

summary.en: In a second reading the Mashgiach explains the chapter as speaking of bitachon. People who calculate their budget see children as a burden, and secular Israelis mock large families, but for a G-d-fearing Jew each child is a blessing that opens a new channel of parnassah; he tells how this was so in his own home. Children are 'like arrows in a warrior's hand', helping their parents.

title.en: The precious years of youth

summary.en: The Mashgiach brings the words of the Kotzker and a letter of the Chiddushei HaRim to his grandson: one year of youth is worth many later years. A young person can still bend his middos like a young tree and retains what he learns; once youth passes, like an arrow shot from the bow, it cannot be recaptured.

title.en: A quiver full of children, and the muddy floor

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains 'fortunate is the man who fills his quiver' as a home full of children who will be arrows in avodas Hashem, and adds a light pshat that even the mud children bring into the house is a great blessing. He tells of a tzaddik in self-imposed galus whose muddy shoes upset a rebbetzin, and his reply that she had mercy on the floor instead of on people, and concludes that one needs priorities.

title.en: Ashrei kol yerei Hashem: the honest Jewish home

summary.en: Turning to chapter 128, the Mashgiach brings the Radak that 'kol' includes the woman, and Rav Samson Raphael Hirsch's reading that David takes a stranger into a Jewish home and town to show its warmth and contentment. He explains 'the toil of your hands' as honestly earned bread, and with the Gemara reads 'fortunate' as this world and 'good for you' as the World to Come.

title.en: The fruitful vine and the olive saplings

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains the modest wife who is content within the home and on whom the whole house stands, and the children like evergreen olive saplings around the table, with a family that eats together and needs no outside sensations. He concludes that only for a yerei Hashem is all this a blessing; to others it means nothing.

catalogTitle: שיר המעלות אשרי כל ירא ה'

oneLiner.en: Learning Tehillim 128 and 129, the Mashgiach explains that one who fears Hashem sanctifies even his physical life and his home, which draws its blessing from the beis medrash and Tziyon, while the nations' hatred of Tziyon comes from envy and leaves them without roots or blessing.

abstract.en: The Mashgiach opens Tehillim 128 with 'haholech bidrachav': the covenant with Noach was a heavenly sign, while the covenant of milah lets a Jew serve Hashem with his very body. Walking in Hashem's ways, even while still on the way, makes the body a sanctuary. He reads the blessings of the Jewish home: the wife as a vine that cannot be grafted, the children rooted at home who bear fruit outside, and the content man who is never bored. With Rav Hirsch he adds that the home's root is the beis knesses, 'Hashem will bless you from Tziyon', and stresses seeing the good of Yerushalayim, with stories of the Chasam Sofer and Rav Yosef Chaim Sonnenfeld and a warning about false zealotry. Turning to Tehillim 129, he describes Jewish suffering since its youth, the empires that vanished, and the nations' envy, the true reason for their hatred. Their end is grass on the roofs, without roots and without blessing, which Rav Shmelke of Nikolsburg applies to those who hate talmidei chachamim, illustrated by a story from Belz.

en: The covenant with Noach was a sign in the heavens, while the covenant of milah lets a Jew serve Hashem with his physical body, which the bnei Noach cannot do.
'Haholech bidrachav' means that one who fears Hashem is praiseworthy even while still on the way, and by walking in Hashem's ways his body becomes a sanctuary for Him.
The man who fears Hashem is content in his home and never bored, unlike those who chase sensations outside.
The beis knesses and beis medrash are the main part of a Jew's home, and from there the private home draws its blessing, 'Hashem will bless you from Tziyon'.
One must see the good of Yerushalayim; criticism must be constructive, and zealotry is only for one who has checked himself that he means only Heaven's sake.
The nations' hatred of the Jews has no reason in Jewish deeds; it comes from envy, a sense that the Jews are better and have a future.
The haters of Tziyon are like grass on the roofs, without roots or a future, and no one passing gives them a blessing.

title.en: The covenant of Noach and the covenant of milah

summary.en: The Mashgiach opens Tehillim 128 with 'haholech bidrachav' and contrasts the covenant with Noach, a rainbow in the sky, with Avraham's covenant of milah. The mitzvos of the bnei Noach are spiritual only, while milah is a covenant in the flesh, letting a Jew serve Hashem with his physical functions.

title.en: Walking in His ways makes the body a sanctuary

summary.en: The Mashgiach brings the Midrash on 'Uri tzafon uvo'i seiman' about korbanos and the eating of shelamim, physical acts that serve Hashem. He explains that one is a 'holech' even before reaching the goal, as a hava amina in Gemara is also Torah, and that walking in Hashem's ways, being compassionate and gracious as He is, makes the body a sanctuary.

title.en: The vine, the olive saplings and the content man

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains 'eshtecha kegefen poriyah': a vine cannot be grafted, which is the purity of the Jewish home, and with the Radak, a vine planted inside the house sends its fruit outside, as children rooted in the home sanctify Hashem's name outside. The man who fears Hashem is blessed and content with his family, never bored, unlike those who chase sensations.

title.en: The private home and the collective home

summary.en: Following Rav Samson Raphael Hirsch, the Mashgiach says the psalm brings the reader into the Jewish home, where the Shechinah rests. He then explains 'yevarechecha Hashem miTziyon': the beis knesses and beis medrash are the collective home and the main source of blessing, and their spirit, like that of Yerushalayim, is brought into the private home.

title.en: Seeing the good of Yerushalayim

summary.en: On 'ur'eh betuv Yerushalayim' the Mashgiach brings Rav Yosef Chaim Sonnenfeld's call to see the good of Yerushalayim, the sin of the meraglim, and a story of the Chasam Sofer. He tells of two brothers to show that zealotry must be purely for Heaven's sake, and closes the psalm: a home rooted in the beis knesses continues Yiddishkeit for generations, 'shalom al Yisrael'.

title.en: 'Rabbas tzeraruni': oppressed since youth

summary.en: Turning to Tehillim 129, the Mashgiach describes Jewish history as full of decrees and persecution, and asks why great empires bother with a tiny nation. The empires that oppressed the Jews have long vanished, and he explains 'al gabi charshu chorshim' with the image of an ox plowing long furrows without rest.

title.en: Hashem cuts the ropes; hatred born of envy

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that Hashem, being a tzaddik, cut the ropes with which the nations harnessed the Jews to their plow, and the haters of Tziyon will retreat in shame, as Charvona turned around when Haman fell. Going back to the beginning of Jewish history shows no reason for the hatred; citing a commentary on 'vayekan'u vo echav', he says the nations hate the Jews out of envy.

title.en: Grass on the roofs, without a blessing

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains 'yihyu kachatzir gagos': growth on a roof has no soil, dries out before it is pulled, and does not fill the reaper's hand, like the nations who have no roots, no true way of life and no future. Passersby give no blessing to such a crop, as one should bless a Jew at his work.

title.en: Rav Shmelke on gilgulim and the Belzer kugel

summary.en: The Mashgiach brings Rav Shmelke of Nikolsburg: the 'haters of Tziyon' are those who hate the talmid chacham, and a soul reincarnated in food finds its tikkun when a Jew makes a brachah over it, which the hater will not merit. He illustrates this with Rav Sholom of Belz, who had a fallen piece of Shabbos kugel picked up and eaten, and ends that one who loves talmidei chachamim is guided by Hashem to a Jewish table.

catalogTitle: שיר המעלות רבת צררני מנעורי

oneLiner.en: Returning to Tehillim 128, the Mashgiach explains that through the Shabbos and Chanukah lights every Jewish home becomes a Beis HaMikdash that Yerushalayim comes to visit, and that Chanukah is a time of growth in Torah and of thanking Hashem.

abstract.en: The Mashgiach announces Tehillim 129 but returns to 128, which, following Rav Samson Raphael Hirsch, shows the warmth and contentment of the Jewish home, and reads 'Hashem will bless you from Zion' as the shul, the communal home. Since it is Kislev, he turns to Chanukah: following the Sfas Emes, the Chanukah lights are a remembrance of the Mikdash, so each home becomes a Beis HaMikdash and each Jew a kohen, bound to the hidden light of the future. He interprets the name Chashmonaim, explains why the Chanukah light may not be used while the Shabbos light may, and shows that the opening words of the psalm's blessing equal 'ner Shabbos, ner Chanukah' in gematria. Chanukah, like Rosh Hashanah, brings remembrance for the barren, physically and spiritually, and blessing means increase; 'children of your children' are chiddushei Torah that beget further chiddushim. He closes that the root of Chanukah is hallel and thanks.

en: Tehillim 128 depicts the warm, contented Jewish home, and 'Hashem will bless you from Zion' refers to the shul and beis medrash, the communal home from which warmth and Torah are brought into the house.
Since the Chanukah lights are a remembrance of the Mikdash, every Jew who lights them has his home become a Beis HaMikdash and himself become like a kohen.

Both the Shabbos light and the Chanukah light come from the hidden light, but on Shabbos a Jew rises to a higher world, while on Chanukah that light comes down into the weekday of exile, so it may not be used.
Chanukah is a time of remembrance for the barren, both for children and for those whose tefillah or Torah bears no fruit.
'Children of your children' alludes to chiddushei Torah that give rise to further chiddushim, the sign that a chiddush was accepted in Heaven.
The essence of Chanukah is hallel and thanks, which is why the Rambam places the laws of Hallel in the laws of Chanukah.

title.en: The Jewish home and Yerushalayim at Chanukah

summary.en: The Mashgiach goes back from Tehillim 129 to 128 and, following Rav Samson Raphael Hirsch, describes the warm, contented Jewish home and the shul as the communal home. Turning to Chanukah, he brings the Sfas Emes that the Chanukah lights are a remembrance of the Mikdash, so that Yerushalayim comes to visit every Jewish home even on a weekday.

title.en: Matisyahu, the Mikdash and every Jew a kohen

summary.en: Using time, place and soul from Sefer Yetzirah, the Mashgiach shows that Matisyahu is the soul of Chanukah and equals 'Beis HaMikdash' in gematria. He adds that each Jew becomes a kohen at Chanukah, tying this to the hidden light of Moshiach (Bnei Yissaschar), the Baal HaTurim on a kingdom of kohanim, and the Rambam that lighting the menorah needs no kohen.

title.en: The menorah's future light and the name Chashmonaim

summary.en: Following the Rokeach, the Mashgiach explains that the menorah's lighting belongs to the light of the future, while its preparation still needs a kohen. He then brings the Chasam Sofer on the name Chashmonaim and adds his own reading: as Hashem answered Haman by adding Purim, He answered the Greeks, who wanted to abolish chodesh, Shabbos and milah, by adding ner Chanukah, alluded to in the letters of chashman.

title.en: Ner Chanukah and ner Shabbos as family mitzvos

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that ner Chanukah is a mitzvah on the family, 'a light for a man and his household', unlike tefillin, which fits the psalm's picture of the family around the table. Ner Shabbos is also a family obligation, and Shabbos itself is a Beis HaMikdash; the novelty of Chanukah is that this comes on a weekday.

title.en: Why the Chanukah light may not be used

summary.en: The Mashgiach asks why one may not use the Chanukah light, which is from the hidden light, when the Shabbos light is also from the hidden light. He describes learning by the Shabbos candles and the Chazon Ish's Friday-night chiddush, and answers that on Shabbos a Jew is lifted to a higher world, while on Chanukah the future light comes down into the weekday of exile.

title.en: Light in the darkest time; ner Shabbos, ner Chanukah

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that Chanukah comes in the darkest time of the year, when the forces of impurity rule, and that today the public domain invades the Jewish home through television, radio and the internet, so one must light inside. Through ner Shabbos and ner Chanukah a Jew merits Zion even in exile, and he shows that the words of the blessing in the psalm equal 'ner Shabbos, ner Chanukah' in gematria.

title.en: Remembrance of the barren and blessing as increase

summary.en: The Mashgiach brings the Bnei Yissaschar that Chanukah, like Rosh Hashanah, is a time of remembrance for the barren, in body and in spirit, including those whose tefillah or Torah is barren. Following the Maharal, the letters of bracha show increase, and Chanukah, which keeps adding, is a time of increase; the Bnei Yissaschar writes that one who makes chiddushei Torah fulfils pru u'rvu.

title.en: Achitofel's barren Torah and chiddushim that bear fruit

summary.en: The Mashgiach brings the Ba'al Shem Tov's question on the Mishnah that David called Achitofel his rebbe for two things: why is this a kal vachomer? He answers that Achitofel's Torah was barren, while a chiddush that leads another to make a further chiddush makes its author a rebbe; this is 'children of your children', and Chanukah is a time for learning after lighting.

title.en: The root of Chanukah is hallel and thanks

summary.en: The Mashgiach says the main mitzvah of Chanukah is hallel and thanks, as the Gemara says it was fixed for hallel and hoda'ah, and connects this to Mizmor Lesodah, the thanks that remains in the days of Moshiach. He notes that the Rambam waits until the laws of Chanukah to give the laws of Hallel, and closes that one must get used to thanking Hashem for every small thing.

catalogTitle: Emunah - A Hereditary Instinct from the Avos

oneLiner.en: The Mashgiach explains that a Jew's emunah is an inherited instinct, a piece of Avraham Avinu in every Yid that Hashem guards and that can never be lost, and that it comes through the mother as feeling rather than logic.

abstract.en: The Mashgiach compares Avraham Avinu to a seed from which a whole tree grows: every Yid was once in Avraham, and Avraham is now in every Yid. Following the Chiddushei HaRim, the bracha Magen Avraham means that Hashem guards this point of emunah, which can be covered up but never extinguished; a kofer only covers it. Since every Yid has a beginning in Avraham, he also has an end, and he will return. He tells the story of the Ramban's student Avner, who found his name in the middle letters of a verse in Ha'azinu, and explains that only the middle, the temporary part of a Jew, can be lost. He then speaks of the Seder night, when emunah is implanted in children through words and through matzah, wine and the cups, and explains that emunah, being emotion and instinct, comes from the mother. He ends that inherited emunah is not yet the mitzvah of emunah.

en: Like every apple and leaf of a tree that was once in its seed, every Yid was once in Avraham Avinu, and a piece of Avraham is now in every Yid.
The bracha Magen Avraham means that Hashem shields the point of Avraham's emunah in every Yid, so that it can never be extinguished, only covered up.
Whatever has a beginning has an end; since every Yid begins in Avraham, he will ultimately return to his roots and do teshuvah.
On the Seder night emunah is implanted in children, both through telling of Yetzias Mitzrayim and through eating matzah, which the Zohar calls the food of emunah.
Emunah is instinct and feeling rather than logic, and therefore, unlike other traits, it is determined by the mother.
Inherited, instinctive emunah is one way of having emunah, but it is not yet the fulfillment of the mitzvah of emunah.

title.en: A piece of Avraham Avinu in every Yid

summary.en: The Mashgiach compares Avraham Avinu to a seed that holds the whole tree, and explains with the Chiddushei HaRim that Magen Avraham means Hashem guards this point of emunah in every Yid. A kofer only covers it up; since every Yid has a beginning in Avraham he has an end, and when Moshiach comes the hidden spark will flare up.

title.en: The Ramban and his student Avner

summary.en: The Mashgiach tells the story brought in the Kav HaYashar of the Ramban's student Avner, who left Yiddishkeit and challenged the Ramban to show him where he is alluded to in Ha'azinu. The Ramban found his name in the third letters of a verse that speaks of erasing their memory, and Avner did teshuvah and set out to sea in a boat without oars.

title.en: Why the middle letters: a Yid is never lost

summary.en: The Mashgiach asks why the hint was in the middle letters, when one normally reads first or last letters, which contain the whole word. He explains that every Yid has a beginning in Avraham and therefore an end that returns to it, like the Torah reading that starts again from Bereishis; only the middle, the temporary part, can be lost, so even Avner will come back.

title.en: The Avos as a new beginning and the Seder night

summary.en: The Mashgiach recalls that the Avos and Imahos could not have children because they were a new species cut off from the previous generations. He then explains that the Seder night was formed as the night to instill emunah in children, since Yetzias Mitzrayim, in which the Ten Utterances of creation were replayed backwards in the Ten Plagues, is the foundation of emunah.

title.en: Matzah and wine: logic and feeling

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that eating matzah, the food of emunah, internalizes emunah, and that the three matzos correspond to the Avos and the four cups to the Imahos, like the shin of three and four heads on the tefillin. Wheat brings knowledge while wine brings feeling; men lean to logic and women to emotion, and emunah is feeling and instinct.

title.en: Emunah comes from the mother

summary.en: Through a rule of dikduk, dropping the final nun of a root to form a noun, the Mashgiach shows that from 'amen', to believe, comes 'em', mother. Everything else is determined by the father, but Jewishness follows the mother, because emunah is instinct like the spider's web or the beaver's dam. He ends that this inherited emunah, which Magen Avraham guards, is not yet the mitzvah of emunah, to be discussed next time.

catalogTitle: שיר המעלות ממעמקים קראתיך ה'

oneLiner.en: The Mashgiach explains the kapitel Shir Hamaalos Mimaamakim as a cry from the hidden depth of the Jewish soul, which sin never reaches, and as the song of a Jew who keeps waiting for the geulah through every disappointment.

abstract.en: The Mashgiach opens with Hirsch's view that this kapitel is the climax of the Shir Hamaalos: Hashem frees Jews even from their sins. Citing the Bnei Yissaschar that teshuvah does not help for the nations, he explains that Jews are children of Hashem, and the point of G-dliness in a Jew's heart is never touched by sin. He supports this from the Rambam on 'until he says I want', and from the thirty-nine lashes. He then reads the kapitel verse by verse: tachanunim as a request for an undeserved gift, forgiveness created before the world, the Jew's direct access to Hashem without intermediaries, and how forgiveness removes the barrier that blocks fear of Heaven. On 'kivisi Hashem' he speaks of daily disappointments in avodah and in the hope for Moshiach, the dates of the ketz that passed, the frum Jews whose machlokes delays the geulah, and the call to keep hoping.

en: This kapitel is the climax of the Shir Hamaalos: beyond saving Jews from physical troubles, Hashem frees them from their sins.
Jews are children of Hashem, and the point of G-dliness in the depth of a Jew's heart is never reached by sin; this depth is the 'maamakim' from which the Jew calls.
A Jew comes to Hashem for forgiveness directly, like a child to his father, without the intermediaries needed before a human king.
Sins form a barrier between a person and Hashem that blocks fear of Heaven; forgiveness removes it, which is why forgiveness leads to fear of Hashem.
A Jew must keep hoping after each disappointment, in his own avodah and in waiting for the geulah, like watchmen waiting for the morning.
Times for the ketz passed without the geulah because they were times of 'achishenah', dependent on merit, and the geulah was spoiled.
