title.en: Why Hashem frees Jews from sin

summary.en: The Mashgiach brings Hirsch's view that this kapitel is the climax of the Shir Hamaalos, since Hashem frees Jews even from their sins, and asks why. From the Bnei Yissaschar he shows that teshuvah does not help the nations, and explains that Jews are children of Hashem, carrying a point of G-dliness that sin does not touch.

title.en: The inner will and the depths

summary.en: The Mashgiach brings the Rambam on forcing a person until he says 'I want', explaining that every Jew inwardly wants Hashem's will. He speaks of the hidden part of the Torah that the Arizal permitted to reveal, and of the thirty-nine lashes that do not reach the highest level of the soul, then reads 'mimaamakim' as calling from that depth.

title.en: Tachanunim: asking for an undeserved gift

summary.en: On 'Hashem shim'ah bekoli', the Mashgiach brings Rashi that tachanunim means asking for an undeserved gift, and the Midrash of the treasure of matnas chinam shown to Moshe Rabbeinu, which opens only to one who knows nothing is due to him. On 'im avonos tishmor' he notes that even the greatest tzaddikim had a flaw.

title.en: Forgiveness before the world; no intermediary

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that since man is prone to sin from Adam on, forgiveness was created before the world. On 'ki imcha haselichah' he contrasts the intermediaries needed before a king, and the confession of the gentiles, with a Jew who comes straight to Hashem as a child, and reads Kayin's 'gadol avoni minso'.

title.en: Forgiveness so that You be feared

summary.en: The Mashgiach brings the Berditchever's words that Hashem is full of mercy greater than man's sins, and explains 'lema'an tivareh': without forgiveness a sinner would despair and give himself over to this world. He then explains that sins are a barrier that keeps a person from feeling Hashem, and forgiveness removes it so he can fear Hashem.

title.en: Kivisi Hashem: hope after disappointment

summary.en: On 'kivisi Hashem' the Mashgiach describes the great day when the whole world will recognize Hashem, and the daily and weekly disappointments of a Jew who resolves to serve Hashem and falls again. He tells how the Sassover Rebbe would resolve each morning to begin anew, and reads 'mishomrim laboker' as waiting for the personal and general geulah.

title.en: Waiting for Moshiach; be'itah and achishenah

summary.en: The Mashgiach tells how the Yismach Moshe waited for Moshiach every moment, including the story of his son's arrival. He then brings the Gemara on 'be'itah achishenah' and the Gemara in Avodah Zarah about a certain year, explaining that the Tannaim's times were times of achishenah, and that at such a time the Satan accuses and brings troubles.

title.en: Dates of the ketz and the spoiled geulah

summary.en: The Mashgiach goes through dates that were foretold for the geulah and brought great troubles instead, and says the geulah was spoiled not by the irreligious but by machlokes and lashon hara among frum Jews. He brings the Arizal's date for the great day of judgment, calls for preparing and self-correction, and ends with 'kivisi Hashem': after each disappointment one keeps waiting for the morning.

catalogTitle: קויתי ה' קותה נפשי

oneLiner.en: On the closing verses of Shir HaMa'alos 'MiMa'amakim', the Mashgiach teaches that a Jew keeps hoping and waiting for Hashem and for the geulah even when every awaited 'morning' passes, and that one who takes shelter in Hashem is redeemed even beyond strict judgment.

abstract.en: The Mashgiach reads 'Kivisi Hashem kivsa nafshi' as a call to keep hoping and praying even when a tefillah is not answered. 'Nafshi la-Hashem mishomrim laboker' is the waiting for the geulah: there is a fixed time that must come, and there are 'mornings' when it can come earlier. He speaks of Moshiach ben Yosef and Moshiach ben Dovid, of how little anyone knows about the order of the redemption, and of the Arizal's words about the year 5765. After stories of tzaddikim who foresaw the fall of Russia, he lists awaited dates that passed and answers that a Jew never gives up: 'Yachel Yisrael el Hashem'. Adam's sin and the Golden Calf were failures to wait. The chapter ends with pedus from sins: Hashem, like a king, can rise above judgment for one who takes shelter in Him, as the Akeidah, the extra verse of Tehillim 34, and the story of Rebbi and the ox show.

en: When a tefillah is not answered, a person must keep hoping to Hashem and keep praying.
'Mishomrim laboker' describes waiting for the geulah: a set time must come regardless, but there are 'mornings' when it can come earlier, and when one passes a Jew waits for the next.
Nobody knows exactly how the redemption will unfold; what is certain is the Torah's promise that it will be greater than anything that came before.
Even after many awaited dates have passed, a Jew does not give up hope; hoping, waiting and believing are the essence of Yiddishkeit and the tikkun of the world.
Adam's sin and the sin of the Golden Calf both came from not waiting, and a Jew's whole tikkun is to wait.
Beyond rescue from troubles, 'v'hu yifdeh es Yisrael mikol avonosav' speaks of redemption from sins, the greatest pedus.
Like a king who can pardon, Hashem can rise above strict judgment for one who throws himself upon Him and takes shelter in Him.

title.en: Keep hoping; waiting for the morning

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains 'Kivisi Hashem kivsa nafshi': one who prayed and was not answered must keep hoping and praying. He reads 'mishomrim laboker' as waiting for the geulah, distinguishing a set time that must come (with the Ramban at the end of Haazinu) from earlier times when it can come.

title.en: Two Moshiachs and the unknown order

summary.en: The Mashgiach distinguishes Moshiach ben Yosef, who can come any day, from Moshiach ben Dovid and the full geulah, and connects the two to Moshe Rabbeinu's two comings in this week's sedra. He adds that, as the Rambam says, nobody knows exactly how the redemption will happen.

title.en: The Torah's promise and the Arizal on 5765

summary.en: What is certain is the Torah's promise in Bechukosai and Nitzavim. The Mashgiach cites the Arizal that a great day of judgment will come in 5765, urges taking it seriously, and explains why the Arizal's words carry weight: before Moshiach tzaddikim greater than their generation can appear.

title.en: Tzaddikim who foresaw Russia's fall

summary.en: The Mashgiach tells of R' Elya Roth in Yerushalayim, who said Russia would soon crumble, and of the Stoliner Rebbe R' Yochanan, who said Russia would last seventy years. He adds R' Elya Roth's tradition that Christianity cannot last more than two thousand years, and a tzaddik's custom of wishing Jews a good year on the gentile New Year.

title.en: When the awaited morning passes

summary.en: The Mashgiach lists awaited times that brought troubles instead of redemption: the Zohar's year 5408, the Malbim's calculation of 1914, a year in the 5700s, and 5746. He asks whether a Jew then gives up, and answers with 'Yachel Yisrael el Hashem': Yiddishkeit is hoping, waiting and believing.

title.en: Adam, the Calf and the Malbim: a Jew waits

summary.en: Hashem too waits impatiently to help His people. The Mashgiach shows that Adam's sin was not waiting for Shabbos and the Golden Calf was not waiting for Moshe, so a Jew's tikkun is to wait. He tells how the Malbim explained to his students that the maskilim 'can do more' than he can.

title.en: Pedus from sins and the transfer of decrees

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that the chapter's last verse speaks of redemption from sins, greater than rescue from troubles. One who finds favor before Hashem can have his decrees transferred to another, as with the se'ir hamishtalei'ach, kaparos on Erev Yom Kippur, 'nasati koferecha Mitzrayim' and the ransom paid for a goring ox.

title.en: Rising above judgment: Tehillim 34 and the Akeidah

summary.en: Hashem runs the world by judgment, but like a king He reserves the right to pardon. The Mashgiach shows this in Tehillim 34, whose alphabet maps the order of creation and judgment, while the extra verse 'Podeh Hashem nefesh avadav' stands outside it. He explains the Akeidah as chesed binding din, renewed each Rosh Hashanah and Yom Kippur.

title.en: Rebbi and the ox: asking asylum from Hashem

summary.en: The Mashgiach tells the Gemara of the ox that fled to Rebbi and the suffering that followed, and a ba'al mussar's question why Rebbi was punished if he was right. The answer: one who asks asylum must be saved. A Midrash parable of a man who claimed to be the king's relative shows that whoever takes shelter in Hashem cannot be held guilty.

catalogTitle: שיר המעלות לדוד ה' לא גבה לבי

oneLiner.en: Through the last verses of Tehillim 130 and the opening of Tehillim 131, the Mashgiach teaches that no tefilah is ever lost, that Jews keep hoping for the geulah through every disappointed date, and that Hashem redeems His children even beyond what they deserve.

abstract.en: The Mashgiach continues Tehillim 130 with 'Kivisi Hashem... v'lidvaro hochalti'. Moshe Rabbeinu davened 515 tefillos and was told to stop one short; that missing tefilah is completed by the tefillos of Klal Yisrael, so one whose prayer is not answered keeps davening. From the Yitav Lev he shows that Hashem told Avraham about Sedom so that his unanswered tefilah would be stored for his children. Times of geulah pass without visible result, as with Achashverosh's and Daniel's calculations and the dates spoken of in later generations, yet a Jew waits for the next 'morning'. 'V'harbeh imo fedus' and 'v'hu yifdeh es Yisrael mikol avonosav' teach that Hashem can redeem even the unworthy, as at Purim, a great eis ratzon that must not be wasted on wild drunkenness. He closes on Tehillim 131: Dovid did not seek grandeur for himself, only for the Beis HaMikdash.

en: One tefilah was missing from Moshe Rabbeinu's 516, and the tefillos of Klal Yisrael over the generations add up to it; so one whose prayer is not answered keeps davening.
A tefilah that cannot help now is kept in reserve for a later time, as Hashem told Avraham about Sedom so his prayer would be stored for his descendants.
Times of geulah come and pass without a visible result, and even the greatest, like Daniel, did not understand the calculations; a Jew keeps waiting for the next morning.
'V'harbeh imo fedus' and 'v'hu yifdeh es Yisrael mikol avonosav' teach that when the time of geulah comes Hashem redeems Klal Yisrael even if they are not worthy.
Purim was a miracle of chesed beyond the people's deeds and is a greater eis ratzon than any other time, which the yetzer hara tries to waste on wild drunkenness.
Dovid HaMelech did not seek the grandeur of a king for himself, only for the Beis HaMikdash, and the Mashgiach warns against building luxurious houses in galus.

title.en: Moshe's missing tefilah and davening again

summary.en: Resuming at 'Kivisi Hashem', the Mashgiach brings that Moshe Rabbeinu davened 515 tefillos and was stopped one short, because Hashem knew what was better for Klal Yisrael; that missing tefilah is completed by Jews' tefillos over the generations, so one who is not answered must daven again.

title.en: Avraham's tefilah kept in reserve

summary.en: The Mashgiach brings the Yitav Lev on 'hamechaseh ani me'Avraham': Hashem told Avraham about Sedom although his tefilah would not help, so that it would be stored for his descendants. He reads 'v'lidvaro hochalti' as waiting for Hashem's word in later times, and notes that times of geulah have passed without our understanding what happened.

title.en: Achashverosh's and Daniel's calculations

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains the Gemara in Megillah that Achashverosh counted the seventy years, saw the Jews not redeemed and made his feast, because a goy cannot bear the Beis HaMikdash, and he applies this to the nations' attitude to Yerushalayim today. He adds that Daniel too erred in the calculation and was told the matters are sealed.

title.en: Pekidah, eis ratzon and the hidden ketz

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that the seventy years were a pekidah, an eis ratzon in which a little more davening, learning and ehrlichkeit can bring Moshiach early, while the fixed day is known only to Hashem. The Satan uses such times to recall sins, and this explains why Haman's decree came seventy years after the bowing to the image.

title.en: Dates that passed, and waiting for the morning

summary.en: The Mashgiach describes the dates for which geulah was expected: the founding of the state, which he calls an imitation diamond with some advantages but nothing from the side of geulah; the year the Satmar Rav cried out to do teshuvah; and the date spoken of by the Arizal, for which one must prepare. He tells of the Blazhever Rav who turned pale at a joke that Moshiach had come, and reads 'nafshi la'Hashem mishomrim laboker' as waiting for morning after morning.

title.en: 'V'harbeh imo fedus': redemption beyond merit

summary.en: On 'yachel Yisrael el Hashem... v'harbeh imo fedus' the Mashgiach brings that 'pedus' is written full here, alluding to the complete redemption of the third Beis HaMikdash, and that 'v'hu yifdeh es Yisrael mikol avonosav' means that when the time comes Hashem redeems even the unworthy. He describes Hashem's way of making a substitute, as with the se'ir la'azazel, kaparos, and 'nasati chofrecha Mitzrayim'.

title.en: The extra pei and Purim's chesed

summary.en: The Mashgiach shows that two alphabetical chapters of Tehillim end with an extra verse of pedus after the alef-beis of reward and punishment: a higher conduct in which Hashem redeems His children even when they do not deserve it. Purim was such a miracle despite the people's sins, and the week's sedra shows the same with the machatzis hashekel atoning and the revealing of the thirteen middos.

title.en: Purim as an eis ratzon, and drinking

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that the Purim miracle came from Hashem's chesed, not the people's deeds, so on Purim one gives to whoever stretches out a hand, and it is a greater eis ratzon than any time of the year. He laments that the yetzer hara turns it into wild drunkenness, contrasts the Gemara's account of how the nations and the Jews behave when they drink, and discusses the views on drinking on Purim.

title.en: 'Lo gavah libi': Dovid's humility and fancy houses in galus

summary.en: The Mashgiach begins Tehillim 131: Dovid HaMelech, unlike other kings, did not seek grandeur and luxury for himself, only for the Beis HaMikdash. From here he brings the Shelah and Sefer Chassidim, who warn against building fine stone houses in galus, and says a house should be comfortable for the family and for learning, while the Beis Hashem must be beautiful.

catalogTitle: The Wonders of the World Point to a Creator

oneLiner.en: The Mashgiach shows that the wonders of creation, down to the human body, plainly point to a Maker, and that denial of Him comes from rationalization, not from knowledge.

abstract.en: The Mashgiach opens by recalling that emunah is an inheritance from the Avos and that a Jew believes instinctively unless he tries to deny it. Such denial is rationalization: Esav blamed his wives for losing the brachos, idol worshippers sought permission for forbidden relations, and Chazal read 'do not stray after your heart and your eyes' as heresy and immorality, because lust leads a person to justify himself with kefirah. He tells the story he once told ten-year-olds about two Africans who explained a watch with bugs chasing cheese, likening it to scientists' changing theories, while the Maker's own account is in the Torah. The kashas are weak; the Chovos Halevavos's mashal of a painting made by a splash of paint shows the absurdity, and Dovid HaMelech sings of creation's wonders. From the human body, the foot and the S-shaped spine, one sees the Creator. He ends with a Yemenite woman who doubted a spaceship, showing there is no conflict between absolute knowledge and Torah, only between theories and Torah.

en: A Jew believes in Hashem instinctively; denial comes only when he tries to deny it.
Kefirah is rationalization: a person who wants to follow his desires looks for a justification and finds it in denying the Torah.
Scientists' theories of how the world came about keep changing, while the Maker Himself wrote the account of creation in the Torah.
Every part of the world, and every detail of the human body, shows that there is a Maker who made it and controls it.
There is no contradiction between absolute scientific knowledge and the Torah, only between changing theories and the Torah.

title.en: Denial as rationalization

summary.en: The Mashgiach recalls that emunah is inherited from the Avos and that a Jew believes instinctively. He shows that denial is rationalization: Esav blamed his wives for losing the brachos, and Chazal read 'after your heart and your eyes' as heresy and immorality, since desire leads a person to justify himself with kefirah.

title.en: The Africans and the watch

summary.en: The Mashgiach tells the story he once told ten-year-olds who had been taught evolution: two Africans explained a watch with bugs chasing cheese and 'proved' it by hearing them stamp. He likens this to scientists who publish ever-changing theories of how the world came by itself.

title.en: The Maker's own book and the painting

summary.en: As Rabbi Pinkus told the Africans to read the watchmaker's book, the Mashgiach says the Maker wrote the account of creation in Sefer Bereishis, but people avoid it because it obligates them. The kashas are weak; he brings the Chovos Halevavos's mashal of a masterpiece made by a splash of paint, and Dovid HaMelech's song of the wonders of creation.

title.en: Seeing the Creator in the human body

summary.en: Citing Iyov's 'from my flesh I see G-d', the Mashgiach describes a diagram of the foot at a doctor's office and an anatomy textbook full of wonders, and explains why the spine is shaped like an S. Medicine assumes everything in the body has a purpose; such wonders cannot come from an explosion.

title.en: The Yemenite woman and the spaceship

summary.en: The Mashgiach tells of a Yemenite Jewish woman who denied the first spaceship because the gates of heaven are in Yerushalayim, having not learned Rashi. He concludes that absolute knowledge never conflicts with the Torah, only theories do, and that denying the Creator is rationalization by people too weak to keep the Torah.

catalogTitle: המשך ה' לא גבה לבי

oneLiner.en: Continuing with Tehillim 131, the Mashgiach explains David HaMelech's humility and contentment, contrasts the inner purpose behind the splendor of true tzaddikim with the craving to show off, and draws from Shimi ben Gera's curse and from Tehillim 132 how David accepted everything from Hashem while toiling for Klal Yisrael.

abstract.en: The Mashgiach reads Tehillim 131, 'Hashem, my heart was not haughty', as the words of a king who was the great anav, alongside Moshe and Avraham. He tells how the Bluzhever Rav never lifted his eyes above the small aron kodesh and so never saw a broken mechitzah. He explains that tzaddikim of the house of David, like the Ruzhiner, conducted themselves with royal splendor for the honor of Heaven while being truly lowly, unlike Achashverosh's feast, made only to display wealth, a klipah he sees in today's luxury. He urges contentment in one's spiritual level, describes a person as a weaned child who trusts that what he lacks he does not need, and praises accepting disgrace as atonement. David's silence before Shimi ben Gera made him the fourth leg of the Divine chariot and brought about Purim. Finally he begins Tehillim 132: David's toil to find the place of the Beis HaMikdash.

en: David HaMelech, though a king, was the great anav, one of the three role models of humility of Klal Yisrael with Moshe and Avraham.
The royal splendor of true tzaddikim from the house of David had an inner purpose of kavod shamayim, while they themselves took nothing from this world.
Spending on luxury in order to be seen is the klipah of Achashverosh, and the Mashgiach says it arouses jealousy among the nations.
A person should know his level, be content with it and not reach for greatness beyond him, even in avodas Hashem.
Like a weaned child with its mother, a Jew trusts that what he needs Hashem gives him, and what he lacks is a sign he does not need it.
Disgrace atones for sins without sickness or poverty, so one should thank Hashem for it.
By bearing Shimi ben Gera's curses in silence as decreed from Heaven, David became the fourth leg of the Divine chariot and merited Purim through Mordechai, Shimi's descendant.

candidateTopics: tzaddikim of the house of David
trust in Hashem like a weaned child

title.en: David the king as the great anav

summary.en: The Mashgiach reads 'Hashem, my heart was not haughty' and explains that David, a king, did not seek great things. He brings the Chasam Sofer's instruction to his children and the words of Moshe, Avraham and David as the three models of humility.

title.en: The Bluzhever Rav and the broken mechitzah

summary.en: The Mashgiach tells how the Shinover Rav, visiting the Bluzhever Rav, asked why the women's mechitzah had a broken hole, and the Bluzhever answered that he never lifted his eyes above the low aron kodesh. This illustrates 'my eyes were not lofty'.

title.en: Royal splendor of the house of David

summary.en: The Mashgiach describes the legendary wealth of the Ruzhiner, who said at his passing that he had no pleasure from this world, and explains that souls of the house of David must carry royalty while being truly humble. He tells of the Ruzhiner standing barefoot in the cold at Kiddush Levanah in soleless shoes, and brings Rebbi's wealthy table from the Gemara.

title.en: Achashverosh's feast and the urge to display

summary.en: The Mashgiach distinguishes the inner intent of true tzaddikim from the show of Achashverosh, whose feast was made to display his wealth and his queen. He calls today's growing luxury, ever finer menorahs and taller shtreimels, a klipah of showing off.

title.en: Wealth without display

summary.en: The Mashgiach says comfort for wealthy Jews is fine, but luxury that dazzles the eye arouses the nations' jealousy, as the Shelah and the Chasam Sofer cry out. He shows that an extra million and a half spent on luxury gives pleasure for only two or three weeks.

title.en: Content with one's level, like a weaned child

summary.en: The Mashgiach applies 'I did not walk in great things' to spiritual life: one should strive according to his own abilities, not envy another's level, and recognize that greater levels come from Hashem. He then explains the second verse, the weaned child who trusts its mother, linking it to 'Hashem is my shepherd, I shall not lack'.

title.en: Equanimity toward honor and disgrace

summary.en: The Mashgiach brings the Chovos HaLevavos on the trait of equanimity, where honor and disgrace are the same, and stresses that it is a level for great tzaddikim. Still, everyone can stop chasing honor and see disgrace as an atonement that spares sickness and poverty, for which one should thank Hashem.

title.en: Shimi ben Gera and the fourth leg of the chariot

summary.en: The Mashgiach tells how David, fleeing Avshalom, forbade Yoav to kill Shimi ben Gera, saying Hashem told him to curse, though Shimi was a rebel against the kingdom. Citing the Tomer Devorah, he says that at that moment David became the fourth leg of the Divine chariot, and that sparing Shimi brought Mordechai and Purim.

title.en: Remember for David all his affliction

summary.en: The Mashgiach begins Tehillim 132: David prepared for the Beis HaMikdash though his son would build it, and his foundations still stand. Hashem remembers all his suffering, for the Satan opposes one who strives for good, and David swore not to rest until he found the place Yaakov had designated.

catalogTitle: להנוסעים לארץ ישראל - מעלת וקדושת הארץ

oneLiner.en: Speaking to those about to travel, the Mashgiach explains that Eretz Yisroel is the Shabbos of the world and that one must prepare for it, long for it and work to merit it.

abstract.en: Speaking to people about to travel to Eretz Yisroel, the Mashgiach describes the land's greatness and how to approach it. Eretz Yisroel is the root of the world as Rosh Hashana is of the year; it is the Shabbos of the world, and Yerushalayim is the Shabbos of Eretz Yisroel. The Torah was given for this land, and a Jew there receives a higher neshama, so both good and bad grow stronger. One must therefore prepare to enter it as one prepares for Shabbos: not as a tourist, but with holiness, longing and tefillah, knowing that the yetzer hara there is greater. He brings stories of Reb Mendel Vitebsker, the Bas Ayin and the Ohr HaChaim, the Chasam Sofer on Moshe Rabbeinu's last tefillah, and closes with Yerushalayim, the Kosel and a call to use the opportunity well.

en: Eretz Yisroel is the starting point and root of the world, as Rosh Hashana is of the year; it is the Shabbos of the world, and Yerushalayim is the Shabbos of Eretz Yisroel.
The Torah was made for Eretz Yisroel, and the land does not tolerate sin the way other lands do.
A Jew who comes to Eretz Yisroel receives a higher neshama, as on Shabbos, so a tzaddik becomes greater and a rasha worse.
One cannot enter Eretz Yisroel casually; it requires preparation of holiness, just as one must prepare for Shabbos and the Yamim Tovim.
A healthy Jew longs for Eretz Yisroel as a healthy body has appetite; lacking that longing is a sign that something is wrong.
One can be in Eretz Yisroel and not merit it; meriting it takes tefillah and a struggle with obstacles and a greater yetzer hara.
A tefillah in Eretz Yisroel, and above all in Yerushalayim at the Kosel, is far greater than one elsewhere.

candidateTopics: eretz yisroel as the shabbos of the world
preparing for a trip to eretz yisroel

title.en: Eretz Yisroel, the Shabbos of the world

summary.en: The Mashgiach opens with the passuk that Hashem's eyes are always on Eretz Yisroel: as Rosh Hashana is the root of the year, the land is the starting point of the world and its Shabbos, and Yerushalayim is the Shabbos of the land. He speaks of the land's special shemirah, says that learning or sinning there carries the weight of Shabbos, and brings the Chasam Sofer that a tzaddik grows greater there and a rasha worse.

title.en: The land of the Torah and a higher neshama

summary.en: Bringing the Ramban and Rashi, the Mashgiach shows that the Torah was made for Eretz Yisroel and that the land cannot bear sin. He explains that a Jew there receives a higher neshama, like the neshama yeseira of Shabbos, citing the Chesed L'Avraham and Yaakov Avinu's angels, and uses the image of a high-voltage wire to explain why both a tzaddik and a rasha grow there.

title.en: Preparing to enter, as for Shabbos

summary.en: The Mashgiach links Shabbos to Yerushalayim through the bracha of Boneh Yerushalayim in bentching, then teaches that one may not enter Eretz Yisroel casually: the people had milah before crossing with Yehoshua, and a Midrash sets conditions of holiness for entering. Just as no one can step into Shabbos straight from a ballgame, one must prepare on Erev Shabbos, each according to his root.

title.en: Ringed by water; being there without meriting it

summary.en: The Mashgiach brings the Ramak that Eretz Yisroel is surrounded by water on all four sides, so entering it is like going to the mikveh before Shabbos. A tourist bathing in the Dead Sea has nothing of the land; just as one who skips the tefillos, kiddush and seudos has no share in Shabbos, one can be in Eretz Yisroel and not merit it.

title.en: Holier than a shul; a longing like for Shabbos

summary.en: The Mashgiach says one cannot play around with Eretz Yisroel: its kedusha exceeds that of a beis haknesses, where one turns one's heart toward the land, so it is the King's palace and not a place for fun. He brings the Sefer Chareidim that a Jew must long for the land, as erliche Yidden long for Shabbos all week.

title.en: A healthy Jew longs for the land

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that Eretz Yisroel, like Shabbos, is called 'chemdah', and that Hashem gave the land He loves to the people He loves. As a healthy body has appetite, a healthy Jew longs for Torah, tefillah and the land: amoraim kissed its stones and rolled in its dust, the Rambam brings this as halacha, and David HaMelech ties the geulah to it. One who lacks the longing must make a cheshbon hanefesh.

title.en: Using the remaining days; obstacles on the way

summary.en: The Mashgiach urges the travelers to use the days left to prepare, as the Torah set preparation before Pesach, Shavuos, Sukkos and Shabbos. Meriting the land is not simple: Moshe Rabbeinu did not merit it, and Rabbi Zeira did not wait for a ferry. From the juxtaposition of Amalek to 'ki savo el ha'aretz' the Chareidim learns that whoever wishes to go meets obstacles, and must fight the yetzer hara and daven.

title.en: Reb Mendel Vitebsker and the yetzer hara

summary.en: The Mashgiach tells how Reb Mendel Vitebsker, a great disciple of the Maggid, told the yetzer hara he had money for only one ticket, so it should stay behind; arriving by ship, he found it waiting, saying the one abroad had only been its messenger. The Mashgiach explains that in Eretz Yisroel, the root of everything, the yetzer hara too is greater, so one must come ready for battle and pay the full price.

title.en: The Bas Ayin in Tzfas; diamonds on the ground

summary.en: After a word on 'eretz chemdah tovah' from bentching, the Mashgiach tells of the Bas Ayin in Tzfas: in the great earthquake his chassidim crowded around him, and the half of his beis medrash where they stood did not collapse, as a plaque there still records. He then tells of a man who as a boy heard that the ground of Eretz Yisroel is covered with diamonds, came and saw none, was told he had not yet merited it, and after secluding himself in avodah rejoiced that he now saw them.

title.en: A diamond, not an acre

summary.en: The Mashgiach contrasts an acre, which is small as land goes, with a diamond the size of an orange, which is enormous: Eretz Yisroel is small next to Russia, America or Egypt, but it is a huge diamond. Only one who believes, davens and toils feels it, as one feels Shabbos or the sweetness of a Gemara; learning in Eretz Yisroel is different, since its air makes one wise.

title.en: Knowing the halachos of the land; new four amos

summary.en: The Mashgiach warns that one must know the mitzvos that depend on the land, terumos and maasros, orlah and shemitah, and be sure of what one eats, since it is easy to stumble. He tells how Reb Yosef Chaim Sonnenfeld would vary his route to gain new four amos in Eretz Yisroel, since each step taken in holiness brings a new share in Torah.

title.en: Moshe Rabbeinu's praise before his last tefillah

summary.en: The Mashgiach brings the Chasam Sofer's question: Moshe Rabbeinu spoke to Hashem face to face, as one familiar, so why only in his last tefillah to enter the land did he open with praise, as Chazal learn from him? He answers that in the land of Sichon and Og, which already had some of the kedusha of Eretz Yisroel, Moshe felt a holiness he had not felt even in heaven, and with it awe before Hashem.

title.en: Yerushalayim, the inner point

summary.en: The Mashgiach returns to Eretz Yisroel as Shabbos and turns to Yerushalayim, the center and inner point of the land, above the portions of the tribes. The Mishnah lets one compel a spouse to move to Eretz Yisroel and from there to Yerushalayim, and Hashem's eyes and heart are there always; since the churban the gates of tefillah are closed, and great merits are needed to break through.

title.en: Tefillah in Eretz Yisroel: Reb Avraham Kalisker's letters

summary.en: The Mashgiach brings the letters Reb Avraham Kalisker sent from Eretz Yisroel to his fellow disciples of the Maggid: at first the land seemed to hide itself, like a prospective kallah who does not show herself, and only later did they merit a tefillah such as they had never davened. The smallest tefillah in Eretz Yisroel is greater than the greatest elsewhere, and over the place of the Mikdash heaven is wide open.

title.en: The kedusha that remains; the Kosel HaMaaravi

summary.en: The Mashgiach mentions the machlokes of the Rambam and Ramban on whether living in Eretz Yisroel is a mitzvah today, and the view that the first kedusha of Yerushalayim remains forever, as 'vahashimosi es mikdesheichem' shows. The Shechinah never left the Kosel HaMaaravi, many have been helped by davening there, and he tells how the Ohr HaChaim sent a poor talmid with a note to place between its stones.

title.en: The Kosel endures; prepare for the great Shabbos

summary.en: The Mashgiach brings the Yismach Moshe that Shlomo HaMelech built knowing that the Kosel would remain after the churban, and that the survival of the Jewish people is bound to it. He closes: what earlier generations longed for in vain is now a plane ticket away, so the travelers should prepare with learning, davening and teshuvah, as before Rosh Hashana, for the great Shabbos of Eretz Yisroel, Yerushalayim and the kivrei tzaddikim.

catalogTitle: חשיבות הליכה לא"י - הכנה והתעוררות לפורים משולש בירושלים

oneLiner.en: Before a group journey to Yerushalayim for Purim Meshulash, the Mashgiach explains that a journey to a holy place is itself a cleansing preparation, describes the holiness of Eretz Yisroel, Yerushalayim and Purim there, and gives practical guidance for traveling with seriousness, calm and derech eretz.

abstract.en: The Mashgiach opens by noting that rabbanim speak about Purim before it, and announces that he will speak about Purim in Yerushalayim, since a journey is coming. A journey to a holy place or a holy person is a great tikkun hanefesh: Avraham was first told to go, the Jews passed through forty-two journeys, and the Ba'al Shem Tov's students traveled to their Rebbe. He warns of the trials of modern travel and stresses guarding the eyes. He then describes the unique holiness of Purim, the honor of Yerushalayim behind walled-city Purim, and Yerushalayim and Purim as places and times of unity. Drawing on 'eretz chemdah', he explains that the Avos and all generations longed for the land, and that a mitzvah there is greater and a sin worse. He closes with practical guidance: no pictures, calm visits, effort in avodah, kiddush Hashem, obeying organizers, and contentment for those who cannot go.

en: The Mashgiach teaches that a journey to a holy place or to a tzaddik is itself a great tikkun hanefesh that prepares the vessels to receive the lights of the place.
Today's travel carries great trials, and guarding the eyes and thoughts on the way is itself part of the preparation for reaching the holy land, city and time.
Walled-city Purim was set from the time of Yehoshua bin Nun to give honor to Yerushalayim, so coming to Yerushalayim for Purim reaches the true intent of Shushan Purim.
Yerushalayim, the concentration of Eretz Yisroel, is the place of unity, and Purim is the time of unity, so Purim in Yerushalayim is the peak of achdus.
A healthy Jewish soul inherits from the Avos a desire for Eretz Yisroel, and all generations longed for it.
A mitzvah done in Eretz Yisroel, and especially in Yerushalayim, is far greater, and a sin there is far worse.
Whether one goes or stays is decreed in Heaven, and one who cannot go should be content with the mission Hashem gives him where he is.

candidateTopics: journeys to tzaddikim and holy places

title.en: A journey to holiness as tikkun hanefesh

summary.en: The Mashgiach notes the custom of speaking about Purim before it and announces he will speak about Purim in Yerushalayim, as a journey is near. He explains that a journey to a holy place or person is a tikkun hanefesh, pointing to the command to Avraham to go and to the forty-two journeys in the desert.

title.en: The Rebbe Reb Elimelech and journeys to tzaddikim

summary.en: The Mashgiach tells of a penitent sent to the Rebbe Reb Elimelech who was told on arrival that the journey had already rectified almost everything. He describes the journeys of the Ba'al Shem Tov's students to their Rebbe, likens them to the forty-two journeys and the days of sefirah, and explains that a journey repairs the vessels so they can receive the lights.

title.en: Old journeys to Meron and today's trials

summary.en: The Mashgiach recalls how people traveled two weeks by donkey from Yerushalayim to Meron with great joy. He warns that today's travel, at airports and on planes, holds great trials, and that guarding the eyes and thoughts turns the journey into a greater preparation, since one sees Tziyon according to the eyes one brings.

title.en: The holiness of Purim and the honor of Yerushalayim

summary.en: The Mashgiach describes the unique holiness of Purim, a new light greater even than Yom Kippur, and Purim as a time when prayer is accepted. He explains that walled-city Purim was set from the days of Yehoshua bin Nun to honor Yerushalayim, which lay in ruins at the time of the miracle, and connects this to Yerushalayim's future wall of fire.

title.en: Yerushalayim and Purim as unity

summary.en: The Mashgiach says that a Jew traveling to Yerushalayim with longing arouses longing above for the rebuilding. Yerushalayim is the place of unity and Purim the time of unity, so traveling together with friends in unity prepares one to receive the lights; perhaps the small efforts of small people will bring the geulah.

title.en: Eretz chemdah: the longing of the Avos

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains 'eretz chemdah' as the land the Avos desired, because their healthy desire sought only true good. A healthy Jew inherits this desire unless he has spoiled it; he brings Avraham, Moshe, Dovid, Amora'im who kissed the stones and rolled in the dust, and the Ramban's words on leaving home for Eretz Yisroel.

title.en: Mitzvos and sins weigh more in Eretz Yisroel

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that a mitzvah in a chosen time or place is multiplied, so a mitzvah in Eretz Yisroel and Yerushalayim is greater and a sin worse; a tzaddik there grows greater and a rasha worse. He speaks of prayers rising there through a thin barrier, the holiness of its fruits, Esav's merit of living in the land, and the merit the land brings in judgment.

title.en: Feeling the holy ground anew

summary.en: The Mashgiach contrasts the mesirus nefesh needed to reach the land before the war with the open doors of today. He brings the Chasam Sofer that the ground of Eretz Yisroel is holier than the heavens of chutz la'aretz, warns that long familiarity dulls the feeling, and says the land should feel new every day, as the Chasam Sofer writes of one who truly understands its holiness.

title.en: Entering the land with awe and purity

summary.en: The Mashgiach brings the Tanya's letter on awakening the old love and says a Jew should feel as if crossing the Yarden with Yehoshua. He brings Rav Hirsch on 'our feet stood' as the frozen awe of a pilgrim, speaks of Purim Meshulash thirty days before Pesach, and brings the Chareidim, from the Ramak, that the land is surrounded by water so one enters it in purity, seriously, as one enters Kol Nidrei.

title.en: No pictures, and visiting with menuchah

summary.en: The Mashgiach warns that taking pictures removes the seriousness of great moments, as at a chuppah, which the Divrei Chaim compared to Rosh Hashanah, and asks that none be taken in Eretz Yisroel. He brings that 'menuchah' refers to Yerushalayim and urges visiting holy places calmly rather than rushing from grave to grave.

title.en: Working for the feeling, and kiddush Hashem

summary.en: Bringing the Ba'al Shem Tov's teaching on davening with a closed heart, the Mashgiach says that at a holy place one does not feel, one should work with emunah, avodah before the gift of feeling. He urges preparing in the coming weeks with Torah, tefillah and sefarim, rejoicing with friends, and asks bochurim to make a kiddush Hashem on the plane by courtesy and helping others.

title.en: Discipline, derech eretz and those who stay

summary.en: The Mashgiach asks the travelers to obey the organizers who work hard, since the trip's success depends on order, and to act with humility and derech eretz. He then turns to those who cannot go because of parents, livelihood or home circumstances, reminding them that Purim teaches nothing is chance and asking them not to cause anyone distress.

title.en: All is from Heaven; closing wishes

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that who goes and who stays is decreed in Heaven, recalling that the Ba'al Shem Tov, the Vilna Gaon and the Chofetz Chaim set out and had to turn back, and asks those who stay to be content with their mission. He closes with wishes to receive the lights of Purim wherever one is, and a short account of a gentile's letter to a Jew he sat beside on a flight.

catalogTitle: “מבשרי אחזה אלקי” - Seeing Hashem Through the Wonders of the Human Body

oneLiner.en: The Mashgiach shows how the eye, heart, lungs, digestion, brain and speech, each a wonder and all dependent on one another, testify that a person can see the Creator from his own body.

abstract.en: The Mashgiach returns to the Chovos HaLevavos's mashal of ink spilled into a poem: nobody would accept it, yet people claim the world made itself. Even if they say no one can be certain, a doubt of one in a hundred would stop anyone from taking a pill from a tainted batch, as the Tylenol scare showed; their denial is rationalization driven by temptation. All of creation proclaims a Creator. He then explains that the point of studying the body is not to list its wonders, which would never end, but to train the mind to see Hashem, as the generation born in the desert marveled at bread growing from the ground. He goes through the eye, the heart, the lungs and the digestive system, stressing that each works automatically and that all depend on each other, then the brain and speech. Every organ has a purpose, so claiming it all happened by itself is a wild imagination that serves only the wish to do as one pleases.

en: Those who deny a Creator do not act this way about real dangers: a one-in-a-hundred doubt keeps anyone from a possibly poisoned bottle, so their denial is rationalization born of temptation.
The purpose of looking at the body is not to list its wonders but to train the mind, which takes everything for granted, to see Hashem everywhere.
The eye is a camera finer than any made, with automatic cleaning, protection and light adjustment.
The eye depends on the heart, the heart on the lungs, and all on the digestive system; each is a wonder and their working together is a further wonder.
Every part of the body has a purpose, so saying it all happened by itself is a wild imagination that serves the wish to do as one pleases.

title.en: Denying a Creator is rationalization

summary.en: The Mashgiach recalls the Chovos HaLevavos's mashal of spilled ink forming a poem, and uses the Tylenol poisoning scare to show that nobody takes a one-in-a-hundred risk; denying a Creator is rationalization driven by temptation, while all of creation proclaims there is a Creator.

title.en: Training the mind to see; the eye

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that looking at the body is meant to train the mind to see Hashem, like the generation born in the desert who marveled at bread growing from the ground. He then describes the eye: a camera finer than any made, with automatic tears, eyelashes, reflexes, pupil adjustment and two eyes for depth.

title.en: The eye needs the heart and lungs

summary.en: The Mashgiach shows that the eye depends on blood for food and for removing wastes, which leads to the heart, a boneless piece of flesh that pumps for decades and speeds up by itself when a person runs. The heart in turn needs the lungs for oxygen, which also adjust their pace automatically.

title.en: The digestive system and interdependence

summary.en: The Mashgiach describes the teeth, the tongue and its taste buds, the many colors and tastes Hashem gave food, swallowing and the stomach's acids, and asks why the stomach does not digest itself. He concludes that heart, lungs and digestion are each a wonder and all interdependent.

title.en: Brain, speech, and 'from my flesh'

summary.en: The Mashgiach describes the brain cells that are never replaced so that memory endures, and the wonder of speech, applying 'from my flesh I see G-d' to a person's own body. He notes that medicine keeps finding a purpose for every organ, calls the denial rationalization, and closes that the aim is to train the mind to see Hashem in all of creation.

catalogTitle: י"ז תמוז - זמן לתקן הפגם של - "וימאסו בארץ חמדה". טעם להחלשת החיבה לא"י בזמננו והתעוררת לעוררה

oneLiner.en: The Mashgiach explains that the exile came from the sin of 'they despised the desirable land', that the days of Bein HaMetzarim are the time to repair it by reawakening the old love for Eretz Yisroel, and why that love has cooled in recent generations.

abstract.en: The Mashgiach opens with the daughters of Tzelofchad, whose love for the land earned them a parshah in the Torah, and with the passuk in Tehillim that the exile was decreed because Klal Yisroel 'despised the desirable land'. The repair, he says, is to cherish Eretz Yisroel as the Avos, Moshe Rabbeinu and the great tzaddikim did, and the Three Weeks are the time for it. He then explains why the longing has weakened: the Zionists took over the land, and the gedolim rightly feared sending people there. He goes on to the greatness of the land: the Torah was given for it, mitzvos and aveiros weigh more there, the unity of Klal Yisroel and the Yamim Tovim depend on it, and its holiness is felt on arrival but must be renewed every day. He ends by noting that the danger of the old Zionists has faded, so ehrliche Yidden may again cherish the land, and prays for the geulah.

en: According to the passuk in Tehillim, the exile among the nations came because of 'they despised the desirable land', and its repair is to cherish Eretz Yisroel.
The Avos, Moshe Rabbeinu and the tzaddikim of all generations longed for Eretz Yisroel, and the days of Bein HaMetzarim call for reawakening that old love.
In the last two generations the longing cooled, partly because the Zionists became the masters of the land and the gedolim feared that people who went there would be spoiled.
The Torah was given for Eretz Yisroel; a mitzvah there is far greater and an aveirah far more destructive than outside the land.
The unity of Klal Yisroel as a people, and with it the Yamim Tovim through the fixing of the months, exist only through Jews living in Eretz Yisroel.
The holiness of Eretz Yisroel is felt strongly on arrival, but a Jew there should feel it anew every day, as with Torah and mitzvos.
Today the danger that came from the old Zionists has faded, and ehrliche Yidden who learn Chumash and Rashi are the ones who still long for the land.

candidateTopics: Zionism and the weakening of longing for the land
Kiddush HaChodesh and the Yamim Tovim

title.en: The daughters of Tzelofchad and the despised land

summary.en: The Mashgiach opens with the daughters of Tzelofchad, whose love of the land earned them a parshah, and with the inner greatness of the Three Weeks. He brings the passuk in Tehillim that the exile was decreed for 'they despised the desirable land', and says the repair is to value and rejoice in Eretz Yisroel.

title.en: The land of desire and the longing of the Avos

summary.en: The Mashgiach brings Pirkei d'Rabbi Eliezer that Eretz Yisroel is to the lands what Shabbos is to the days, and describes the longing of the Avos and Moshe Rabbeinu's many tefillos to enter. He brings the Sifrei that dwelling in the land equals all the mitzvos and Rabbi Abba kissing the stones of Acco, and calls for reawakening the old love in these days.

title.en: The great ones who yearned for the land

summary.en: The Mashgiach says our generation lacks the longing of earlier tzaddikim, and brings the Ramban, the Chasam Sofer and the Chofetz Chaim, who was held back by Heaven when he was already packed to go. He explains that great people were not let in because their tefillos there would have brought the geulah, and cites the Ramban's and the Vilna Gaon's words of longing.

title.en: Why the love cooled: the Zionists

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that in the last two generations the longing cooled because the Zionists became masters of the land and the gedolim feared people would be spoiled there, so ehrliche Yidden came to feel a resistance to it. He brings the Shomer Emunim and Rav Yosef Chaim Sonnenfeld, who says the meraglim foresaw by ruach hakodesh the falling generations in the land.

title.en: Greater holiness, greater danger

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that the yetzer hara in Eretz Yisroel is greater, so the land is not for everyone, and a mitzvah or an aveirah there weighs far more. The reason is that the Torah was given for the land, which is why the Avos kept the mitzvos only there, and why the dor hamidbar should have gone in with simple trust.

title.en: Unity of the people and the Yamim Tovim

summary.en: The Mashgiach brings the Sefer Chareidim that one must long for the land, and explains that Jews are one people only through Eretz Yisroel, as seen from the halachah of the 'kahal'. From the Rambam he shows that the months, and so the Yamim Tovim that give a Jew his life of emunah all year, can be fixed only through Jews in Eretz Yisroel.

title.en: Mitzvos in exile as signposts

summary.en: The Mashgiach brings Rashi on 'and you shall place these words' that mitzvos are kept in exile as signposts, so that they will not be new when the Jews return. He then explains that a mitzvah or a blatt Gemara in Eretz Yisroel is worth far more than outside, as Shabbos is to the weekdays, and an aveirah there causes far greater destruction.

title.en: Torah of Eretz Yisroel and the end of idolatry

summary.en: The Mashgiach brings the Midrash that there is no Torah like the Torah of Eretz Yisroel, and says one sees it in the success of those who learn there and the sefarim written there; Yerushalayim is holier still, and one must be careful there. He then explains that the yetzer hara for avodah zarah was nullified only by those who had the merit of the land, Yehoshua and the Anshei Knesses HaGedolah, not by Moshe Rabbeinu.

title.en: A day in Your courts, and fresh holiness

summary.en: The Mashgiach brings 'better one day in Your courts than a thousand' and Rashi's reading of it as a thousand years, and the teaching that living in the land brings a neshamah of holiness. He describes the feeling on arriving, like accepting Shabbos, Rav Chaim Shmuelevitz's experience, and says the feeling fades with habit though every mitzvah should be as new as the day it was given.

title.en: Tefillin, the fruits and the lasting holiness

summary.en: The Mashgiach says a Jew in Eretz Yisroel should feel each day as if he just arrived, and that this freshness is written in the parshiyos of tefillin, which hold the foundations of Yiddishkeit. He speaks of the joy of a brachah on the fruits of the land, and brings the Rambam that the holiness of the Shechinah in the land never ceases, and the Sefer Chareidim that one must honor the land.

title.en: The Zionists then and now, and a closing tefillah

summary.en: The Mashgiach contrasts the old settlers' mesiras nefesh and the old Zionists' remaining longing with today's leaders, for whom the land means nothing, without entering the political question. Only ehrliche Yidden who learn Chumash and Rashi still long for it, and he brings the Chasam Sofer that speaking of the land brings yiras shamayim. He closes by tying it to the Three Weeks and parshas Pinchas and prays for the geulah.

oneLiner.en: Speaking in Jerusalem and then at Kever Rachel, the Mashgiach explains how a Jew must rekindle the ancient love for Eretz Yisroel as if it were given to him today, and why at the grave of Rachel, the mother of Klal Yisroel, one can accomplish everything.

abstract.en: The Mashgiach opens in Jerusalem with the Ba'al HaTanya's call to awaken the ancient love of the Holy Land, a love that must burn like fire, as Rashi says of the gift of the land: as if given today. He traces this longing from the Avos through the Ramban, the Vilna Gaon and the Chofetz Chaim. He explains that only in Eretz Yisroel are Jews a single nation, that it is the gate of heaven where tefillos pass unblocked, and that Jerusalem must never become routine; one must prepare before coming to the Kosel. On the second side, at Kever Rachel, he explains that Rachel weeps for her children throughout the galus, connects Beis Lechem with Yovel and the fifty days to Rosh Hashanah, and brings the Midrash in which Rachel's plea was answered because she overcame jealousy, beginning the repair of the diminished moon.

en: The Mashgiach says the love of Eretz Yisroel must be awakened like a burning fire, as though Hashem gave the land today, and at the very least with some warmth.
Jews have always longed for Eretz Yisroel with self-sacrifice, from the Avos and Moshe Rabbeinu through the Amora'im, the Ramban and the great tzaddikim of later generations.
Eretz Yisroel is the gate of heaven: the clouds that block tefillos are thin there and absent over Har HaBayis, so one must come to Jerusalem and the Kosel prepared and with freshness.
Rachel weeps for her children not only at the churban but throughout the galus, and she is the mother of Klal Yisroel.
At Kever Rachel one can accomplish everything, as by a mother, and it is a fitting place to daven for Klal Yisroel.
Rachel's plea was accepted where the Avos and Imahos were not, because she overcame jealousy and gave over the signs to her sister.

title.en: Awakening the ancient love of the Holy Land

summary.en: Sitting in Jerusalem facing Har HaBayis, the Mashgiach takes the opportunity to speak about Eretz Yisroel. He brings the Ba'al HaTanya's words about awakening the ancient love of the Holy Land and Rashi's teaching that the land should be seen as given today, so that the love burns like fire, or at least with some warmth.

title.en: The longing of the generations for the land

summary.en: The Mashgiach shows the longing for Eretz Yisroel through the generations: the Avos, Moshe Rabbeinu's plea, the Amora'im who kissed its stones, the Ramban's words, and the Vilna Gaon and Chofetz Chaim, whom Heaven held back. He brings the Yalkut that Hashem found no land fit for Israel except Eretz Yisroel.

title.en: A single nation in the land; the gate of heaven

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains from the Sefer Chareidim and the passuk 'goy echad ba'aretz' that only in Eretz Yisroel are Jews one nation, comparing a Jew in chutz la'aretz to an animal in a zoo. He calls the land the gate of heaven, brings the Arizal's constant ruach hakodesh there and the Midrash on 'bezos' as the merit of Jerusalem, and warns that coming to Jerusalem must not become routine.

title.en: Preparing for the Kosel; seeing with the heart

summary.en: The Mashgiach tells of a Rebbe who would not pass the Kosel without preparation, and explains that the clouds blocking tefillos are absent over Har HaBayis. He brings Rav Yosef Chaim Sonnenfeld's words that his only merit was dwelling in the holy city, and closes with the vision of the third Beis HaMikdash on Shabbos Chazon, seen with the heart.

title.en: Interlude; Shabbos niggunim

summary.en: An interlude, with a brief mention of singing Shabbos niggunim.

title.en: Rachel weeps for her children; Beis Lechem and Yovel

summary.en: At Kever Rachel the Mashgiach explains that Rachel weeps for her children throughout the galus, as the mother of Klal Yisroel. He says each part of Eretz Yisroel corresponds to a part of the Torah, and Beis Lechem corresponds to Yovel, the return of each man to his inheritance, which he links to 'veshavu vanim ligvulam' and to the fiftieth day of Matan Torah.

title.en: Fifty days to Rosh Hashanah; Rachel and Moshiach

summary.en: The Mashgiach counts fifty days from after Tisha B'Av to Rosh Hashanah, the day of the shofar like Yovel, and says this is an auspicious time to daven at Kever Rachel, where one can accomplish everything as by a mother. He speaks of Moshiach being revealed nearby at Migdal Eder, of Rachel as the aspect of the Shechinah and of Shabbos, and of tzaddikim who gathered there on Friday to sing Shabbos niggunim. Singing follows.

title.en: Rachel's plea and the repair of the moon

summary.en: The Mashgiach brings the Midrash cited by Rashi: when Menashe placed an idol in the Heichal, the Avos and Imahos could not appease Hashem, but Rachel pleaded that she had overcome her jealousy and given her sister the signs, and she was answered. He explains that Rachel is the aspect of the moon, whose jealousy brought its diminishing, the source of the jealousy and hatred that brought galus, and that Rachel began its repair.

title.en: Closing: Yeshayahu comes to console

summary.en: An interlude, followed by a brief mention of the prophet Yeshayahu coming to console.

oneLiner.en: Speaking at the holy places of Eretz Yisroel, the Mashgiach explains what each place holds: Kever Rachel the softer judgment of the second day of Rosh Hashanah, Ramah the tefillah of Chana, the Me'aras HaMachpela the root of emunah, the Kosel the gate of tefillah, and the Arizal's birthplace the revelation of the hidden light.

abstract.en: The Mashgiach opens with a Midrash: whether the vineyard's wine is good or bad, it belongs to the King, and so the Jewish people remain Hashem's even when they sin; Yeshayahu's 'Nachamu' comforts all generations. At Kever Rachel he explains that Leah is the harsh judgment of the first day of Rosh Hashanah and Rachel the softer judgment of the second; what exists in time exists in place, so here one davens for a good judgment. At Ramah he speaks of Chana, the soul of Rosh Hashanah, and of Shmuel's gilgulim. At the Me'aras HaMachpela, the cradle of emunah, he urges davening like Kalev to be saved from today's 'counsel of the spies', and rejoicing like the Ramban. He calls the Kosel the main post office of tefillah, and at the Arizal's birthplace speaks of the hidden light and a new start in serving Hashem.

en: Like the wine of the King's vineyard, the Jewish people belong to Hashem whether they are good or bad, and this is a chizuk for every Jew who wonders what connection he still has with Hashem.
Kever Rachel is the place of the second day of Rosh Hashanah, the softer judgment, so it is a place to daven for a good judgment for all Jews.
Chana, whose tefillah the Gemara learns many laws of prayer from and whose story is read on Rosh Hashanah, is the soul of Rosh Hashanah, and she rests with Shmuel at Ramah.
The Me'aras HaMachpela, resting place of the Avos, is the root and cradle of emunah, and there one should daven, as Kalev did, to be saved from the 'counsel of the spies' of one's own generation.
The Mashgiach says one should rejoice and make a yom tov over having merited to come to the Me'aras HaMachpela and the Kosel, and use every moment there.
The Kosel is the 'main post office' from which tefillos go up, so the time there should not be wasted.
At the place where the Arizal, a revelation of the hidden light, was born, each person can have a new point of longing and of doing Hashem's will born within him.

title.en: The King's vineyard and Nachamu

summary.en: The Mashgiach brings the Midrash of the King whose vineyard's wine, good or bad, is always his, applies it to Hashem calling the Jews 'My people', and draws chizuk from it. He then brings the Midrash that Yeshayahu's 'Nachamu nachamu ami' comforts all generations.

summary.en: An interlude.

title.en: Kever Rachel and the second day of Rosh Hashanah

summary.en: At Kever Rachel the Mashgiach explains that Leah is the harsh judgment of the first day of Rosh Hashanah and Rachel the softer judgment of the second, when Hashem hears Rachel's weeping. Since what exists in time exists in place, this is the place of the second day, and here one can daven for a good judgment.

summary.en: An interlude at Kever Rachel.

title.en: The haftoros of Rachel and Chana

summary.en: The Mashgiach says the haftorah of the second day of Rosh Hashanah speaks of Rachel and holds more comfort than all of Yeshayahu. At Ramah he calls Chana the soul of Rosh Hashanah and explains Shmuel's gilgulim as Korach and Rabbi Elazar ben Azaryah, which answers 'like seventy years' and Rabbi Elazar's need for wealth; Shmuel was the first navi and Chana the first to call Hashem Tzevakos.

title.en: Me'aras HaMachpela, cradle of emunah

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that, like Kalev who went to Chevron to be saved from the spies, one comes to the Avos, the root of emunah, to be saved from today's 'counsel of the spies': kefirah, pritzus and electronic devices. He brings the Zohar on Yaakov's greatness and the Ramban, who made a yearly yom tov for having davened at the Mikdash and the Machpela.

title.en: The merit of Chevron and the dancing mountains

summary.en: The Mashgiach brings the announcement in the Beis Hamikdash that the east was lit 'until Chevron', to recall the merit of the Avos, tells how the Lelover took the Shinever Rav to Chevron and showed him the mountains dancing, and says the light of Gan Eden that Adam Harishon saw here is why Avraham wanted this cave. He urges using the place to daven for emunah, yiras Shamayim and yeshuos.

title.en: The Kosel, main post office of tefillah

summary.en: The Mashgiach tells of a Jew who toured the holy places each year and, on reaching Yerushalayim, ran to the Kosel calling it the main post office. He says that though one must sit and learn all year, this time should be used to daven there, and a few words of Selichos are sung.

title.en: The Arizal's birthplace and the hidden light

summary.en: At the place where the Arizal was born, the Mashgiach speaks of the sod in every Jew that only Hashem sees, of the Arizal's bond with Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai and the month of Av, and of the soul of the hidden light that came down through Rashbi, the Arizal and the Ba'al Shem Tov. He closes that here each person can begin anew in serving Hashem, with a tefillah for the geulah.

catalogTitle: Hashem Maintains a Balanced World with Breathtaking Precision

oneLiner.en: The Mashgiach shows that people who reject emunah are hiding from what they know, and that the precise balance of the world, from the oxygen in the air to ice floating on water, shows that Hashem maintains His world.

abstract.en: The Mashgiach opens with a letter printed in a newspaper after the Six-Day War, in which a woman asked the editor to stop writing about the miracles because they gave her a guilty conscience about driving to the beach on Shabbos. People, he says, bury their heads in the sand so that emunah will not hinder their desires. He illustrates this with a story the Telzer Rosh Yeshiva, Rav Bloch, wrote in his sefer: a ceiling that kept falling until boards soaked with a suicide's blood were buried, after which one boy stopped coming to the club so as not to see evidence of G-d. The Mashgiach then dismisses fears that the world will be ruined, comparing them to Rashi's account of the Dor Haflagah, and shows Hashem's balance in nature: 21% oxygen, the exchange of oxygen and carbon dioxide, worms and birds, blood clotting, and water, which expands near freezing so that ice floats and fish survive. He ends noting that Jews too have their own pattern of behavior.

en: People do not truly disbelieve; they hide their belief because emunah would hinder their pursuit of desires.
The world cannot be ruined by human progress, because Hashem who made the world controls and maintains it, as a household with a master is in order.
The air always holds 21% oxygen, the exact amount that lets people breathe without the world catching fire, and the carbon dioxide people and animals breathe out feeds the plants.
Nature is balanced throughout: worms soften the earth for plants, birds keep the worms in check, and birds of prey keep the birds in check.
Blood clots only on contact with air, sealing a wound without blocking the veins, a built-in repair system that shows Hashem's wisdom.
Water, unlike other elements, expands as it nears freezing, so ice floats and fish and plants survive beneath it.

summary.en: The Mashgiach describes the miracles of the Six-Day War and a letter to the editor from a woman in Tel Aviv who asked the paper to stop reporting them because they made her feel guilty about going to the beach on Shabbos. He says this shows how people bury their heads in the sand so emunah will not hinder their desires.

title.en: The ceiling that kept falling in the club

summary.en: The Mashgiach tells a story the Telzer Rosh Yeshiva, Rav Bloch, wrote in his sefer: in a club of boys who had left Yiddishkeit, the ceiling kept falling until boards soaked with the blood of a boy who took his life were buried as the Shulchan Aruch requires. One boy then stopped coming so he would not see evidence of G-d, which shows that people hide their belief rather than lack it.

title.en: The balance of the air and of nature

summary.en: The Mashgiach calls fears that pollution and deforestation will ruin the world nonsense, compares them to the Dor Haflagah's fear that the sky would collapse, as Rashi brings, and says Hashem maintains His world. He shows the balance of 21% oxygen, the exchange of oxygen and carbon dioxide between people and plants, and the chain of worms, birds and birds of prey.

title.en: Blood clotting and expansion by heat

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that blood clots only on contact with air, sealing wounds without causing strokes or heart attacks, and notes hemophiliacs who lack this. He then introduces the law that every element expands when heated, using the gaps between railroad tracks.

title.en: Why ice floats

summary.en: After the thermometer, the Mashgiach shows that water alone expands again as it nears freezing, so ice is lighter than water and floats, keeping fish and plants alive beneath it. He closes saying that Jews also have their own pattern of behavior, to be discussed the next week.
